## Statement refuted

Every $u\in H^1_0((0,1)^2)$ belongs to $H^{1+r}((0,1)^2)$ for some
$r\in(1/2,1]$.

1.1 On $0<x<1/4$, writing $c(y)=y(1-y)$, one has $\partial_xu=\tfrac34c(y)x^{-1/4},\qquad \partial_yu=(1-2y)x^{3/4}.$ Everywhere else the cutoff and its derivative are bounded. Since $u$ and $\partial_yu$ are square integrable and $|\partial_xu|^2\le C(1+x^{-1/2})$, the weak first derivatives lie in $L^2(\Omega)$; the classical interior derivatives give the distributional derivatives because test functions are compactly supported away from the boundary. Thus $u\in H^1(\Omega)$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 To prove the zero-boundary condition, let $\theta_\epsilon(t):=\sigma((t-\epsilon)/\epsilon)$. By [F1], it is smooth, zero for $t\le\epsilon$, and one for $t\ge2\epsilon$. Since $\sigma'$ is continuous and vanishes outside $[0,1]$, $\|\theta_\epsilon'\|_\infty\le C/\epsilon$. Set $\eta_\epsilon(x,y)=\theta_\epsilon(x)\theta_\epsilon(y)\theta_\epsilon(1-y)$. Each $\eta_\epsilon u$ is smooth and compactly supported in $\Omega$, since the $x$ cutoff removes the only nonsmooth boundary point and $\chi$ vanishes near $x=1$. Write $u-\eta_\epsilon u=(1-\theta_\epsilon(x))u+\theta_\epsilon(x)(1-\theta_\epsilon(y)\theta_\epsilon(1-y))u$. In the first term, all support lies in $x<2\epsilon$; the squared $L^2$ and derivative errors are bounded by $C\epsilon^{2(3/4)-1}=C\epsilon^{1/2}$, including the $\epsilon^{-1}u$ cutoff derivative. In the second term, support lies in the two strips of width $2\epsilon$ near $y=0,1$. There $|u|\le Cx^{3/4}\operatorname{dist}(y,\{0,1\})$ and its first derivatives are bounded by $Cx^{3/4}+Cx^{-1/4}\operatorname{dist}(y,\{0,1\})$; integrating the strips shows the squared errors and cutoff-derivative terms are $O(\epsilon)$. Thus $\eta_\epsilon u\to u$ in $H^1(\Omega)$, so the closure definition gives $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Choose $0<\delta<1/12$ so small that $c(y')/c(y)\le1.05$ whenever $0<x<\delta$, $1/3\le y\le2/5$, and $y\le y'\le y+x$. For the pairs below, $x'\le3x<1/4$, so both points lie where $\chi=1$; also $c(y)$ is bounded below by a positive constant on this $y$ interval. For $2x\le x'\le3x$ and $y\le y'\le y+x$, the values of $\partial_xu(x,y)$ and $\partial_xu(x',y')$ then differ by at least $\tfrac34c(y)x^{-1/4}\bigl(1-1.05\,2^{-1/4}\bigr).$ Thus $|\partial_xu(x,y)-\partial_xu(x',y')|\ge Cx^{-1/4}$. Also $|(x,y)-(x',y')|\le\sqrt5x$. By [F2], restricting the $H^{1/2}$ Gagliardo integral to these pairs gives a lower bound $C\int_0^\delta x^{-1/2}x^{-3}\,x^2\,dx =C\int_0^\delta x^{-3/2}\,dx=\infty,$ where the two factors of $x$ are the lengths of the $x'$ and $y'$ intervals. Thus $\partial_xu\notin H^{1/2}(\Omega)$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Let $D=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)=\sqrt2$. For $1/2<r<1$ and $x\ne y$, $|x-y|^{-3}=|x-y|^{2r-1}|x-y|^{-2-2r}\le D^{2r-1}|x-y|^{-2-2r}$. Integrating gives $[q]_{H^{1/2}(\Omega)}^2\le D^{2r-1}[q]_{H^r(\Omega)}^2$ for every $q\in H^r(\Omega)$, so $H^r(\Omega)\subset H^{1/2}(\Omega)$. If $u\in H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ for such an $r$, [F4] would imply $\partial_xu\in H^r(\Omega)$ and hence $H^{1/2}(\Omega)$, contradicting step 2.1. Thus no exponent $r\in(1/2,1)$ satisfies the refuted claim. [A1, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]

3.2 It remains to exclude $r=1$. For $0<x<1/4$, the cutoff is one and $-\Delta u=	frac{3}{16}c(y)x^{-5/4}+2x^{3/4}$. On $1/3\le y\le2/5$, $c(y)$ is bounded below by a positive number, so this classical Laplacian is bounded below by $c_0x^{-5/4}$ for some $c_0>0$; its square has divergent integral at $x=0$. Since the distributional Laplacian agrees with this classical function in the open square, it has no $L^2$ representative. By [F5], $u
otin H^2(\Omega)=W^{2,2}(\Omega)$. The example still defines a bounded weak functional on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ by $v\mapsto\int_\Omega
abla u\cdot
abla v$, using Holder [F5]; it does not supply the $L^2$ source assumed by the method. Since the example has no $H^{1+r}$ regularity with $r>1/2$, it does not satisfy the trace hypothesis in [F3], and no normal-gradient trace conclusion is claimed. [A1, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]
4.1 Step 3.1 excludes every $r\in(1/2,1)$, and step 3.2 excludes $r=1$. These are all exponents in the asserted range, so the counterexample refutes the Statement. [step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Statement refuted

Every $u\in H^1_0((0,1)^2)$ belongs to $H^{1+r}((0,1)^2)$ for some
$r\in(1/2,1]$.

1.1 On $0<x<1/4$, writing $c(y)=y(1-y)$, one has $\partial_xu=\tfrac34c(y)x^{-1/4},\qquad \partial_yu=(1-2y)x^{3/4}.$ Everywhere else the cutoff and its derivative are bounded. Since $u$ and $\partial_yu$ are square integrable and $|\partial_xu|^2\le C(1+x^{-1/2})$, the weak first derivatives lie in $L^2(\Omega)$; the classical interior derivatives give the distributional derivatives because test functions are compactly supported away from the boundary. Thus $u\in H^1(\Omega)$. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 To prove the zero-boundary condition, let $\theta_\epsilon(t):=\sigma((t-\epsilon)/\epsilon)$. By [F1], it is smooth, zero for $t\le\epsilon$, and one for $t\ge2\epsilon$. Since $\sigma'$ is continuous and vanishes outside $[0,1]$, $\|\theta_\epsilon'\|_\infty\le C/\epsilon$. Set $\eta_\epsilon(x,y)=\theta_\epsilon(x)\theta_\epsilon(y)\theta_\epsilon(1-y)$. Each $\eta_\epsilon u$ is smooth and compactly supported in $\Omega$, since the $x$ cutoff removes the only nonsmooth boundary point and $\chi$ vanishes near $x=1$. Write $u-\eta_\epsilon u=(1-\theta_\epsilon(x))u+\theta_\epsilon(x)(1-\theta_\epsilon(y)\theta_\epsilon(1-y))u$. In the first term, all support lies in $x<2\epsilon$; the squared $L^2$ and derivative errors are bounded by $C\epsilon^{2(3/4)-1}=C\epsilon^{1/2}$, including the $\epsilon^{-1}u$ cutoff derivative. In the second term, support lies in the two strips of width $2\epsilon$ near $y=0,1$. There $|u|\le Cx^{3/4}\operatorname{dist}(y,\{0,1\})$ and its first derivatives are bounded by $Cx^{3/4}+Cx^{-1/4}\operatorname{dist}(y,\{0,1\})$; integrating the strips shows the squared errors and cutoff-derivative terms are $O(\epsilon)$. Thus $\eta_\epsilon u\to u$ in $H^1(\Omega)$, so the closure definition gives $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Choose $0<\delta<1/12$ so small that $c(y')/c(y)\le1.05$ whenever $0<x<\delta$, $1/3\le y\le2/5$, and $y\le y'\le y+x$. For the pairs below, $x'\le3x<1/4$, so both points lie where $\chi=1$; also $c(y)$ is bounded below by a positive constant on this $y$ interval. For $2x\le x'\le3x$ and $y\le y'\le y+x$, the values of $\partial_xu(x,y)$ and $\partial_xu(x',y')$ then differ by at least $\tfrac34c(y)x^{-1/4}\bigl(1-1.05\,2^{-1/4}\bigr).$ Thus $|\partial_xu(x,y)-\partial_xu(x',y')|\ge Cx^{-1/4}$. Also $|(x,y)-(x',y')|\le\sqrt5x$. By [F2], restricting the $H^{1/2}$ Gagliardo integral to these pairs gives a lower bound $C\int_0^\delta x^{-1/2}x^{-3}\,x^2\,dx =C\int_0^\delta x^{-3/2}\,dx=\infty,$ where the two factors of $x$ are the lengths of the $x'$ and $y'$ intervals. Thus $\partial_xu\notin H^{1/2}(\Omega)$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Let $D=\operatorname{diam}(\Omega)=\sqrt2$. For $1/2<r<1$ and $x\ne y$, $|x-y|^{-3}=|x-y|^{2r-1}|x-y|^{-2-2r}\le D^{2r-1}|x-y|^{-2-2r}$. Integrating gives $[q]_{H^{1/2}(\Omega)}^2\le D^{2r-1}[q]_{H^r(\Omega)}^2$ for every $q\in H^r(\Omega)$, so $H^r(\Omega)\subset H^{1/2}(\Omega)$. If $u\in H^{1+r}(\Omega)$ for such an $r$, [F4] would imply $\partial_xu\in H^r(\Omega)$ and hence $H^{1/2}(\Omega)$, contradicting step 2.1. Thus no exponent $r\in(1/2,1)$ satisfies the refuted claim. [A1, F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]

3.2 It remains to exclude $r=1$. For $0<x<1/4$, the cutoff is one and $-\Delta u=	frac{3}{16}c(y)x^{-5/4}+2x^{3/4}$. On $1/3\le y\le2/5$, $c(y)$ is bounded below by a positive number, so this classical Laplacian is bounded below by $c_0x^{-5/4}$ for some $c_0>0$; its square has divergent integral at $x=0$. Since the distributional Laplacian agrees with this classical function in the open square, it has no $L^2$ representative. By [F5], $u
otin H^2(\Omega)=W^{2,2}(\Omega)$. The example still defines a bounded weak functional on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ by $v\mapsto\int_\Omega
abla u\cdot
abla v$, using Holder [F5]; it does not supply the $L^2$ source assumed by the method. Since the example has no $H^{1+r}$ regularity with $r>1/2$, it does not satisfy the trace hypothesis in [F3], and no normal-gradient trace conclusion is claimed. [A1, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]
4.1 Step 3.1 excludes every $r\in(1/2,1)$, and step 3.2 excludes $r=1$. These are all exponents in the asserted range, so the counterexample refutes the Statement. [step 3.1, step 3.2] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the mesh and coefficient hypotheses of [[def-sipdg-bilinear-form-and-energy-norm]]. Let $e|_K\in H^2(K)$ on every cell, and let $z|_K\in H^2(K)$ be a dual solution with matching interior traces, zero boundary trace, matching normal coefficient fluxes, and $-\nabla\cdot(A_K\nabla z)=e$ on every cell. Then the SIPDG form, extended to these piecewise regular functions by its same formula, satisfies
$$a_h(e,z)=\|e\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, as in the Sobolev interpolation suppliers.

Let $\mathcal T\le\mathcal T_*$ be conforming P1 meshes with exact Galerkin solutions $U,U_*$. Let $\mathcal R=\{K\in\mathcal T:K\text{ is subdivided in }\mathcal T_*\}$ and let $\omega(\mathcal R)$ be the union of the vertex stars of cells in $\mathcal R$. Then
$$\|\nabla(U_*-U)\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2\le C\sum_{K\in\mathcal R}\eta_K(U)^2,$$
where $C$ depends on shape regularity, $|b|h_{\max}$, and the local interpolant constants.

1.1 Define an auxiliary coarse moment map $J:H_0^1(\Omega)	o V(\mathcal T)$ for this nested pair. At each interior vertex $z$, choose the least-index incident coarse cell $L_z
otin\mathcal R$ if one exists, otherwise the original selected cell $K_z$, and use its dual affine moment $q_z(w)=\int_{L_z}w\psi_{z,L_z}$; at boundary vertices use zero. Set $Jw=\sum_{z\ {m interior}}q_z(w)\varphi_z$. The same conforming zero-boundary membership argument as in [F2] applies. Its bounds are uniform: on a cell $K$ use the patch mean $c$ when $K$ misses the boundary and $c=0$ otherwise. Then $q_z(w)-c=\int_{L_z}(w-c)\psi_{z,L_z}$ for interior vertices, while boundary coefficient differences are zero. Because $L_z\subset\omega_K$ and $h_{L_z}\asymp h_K$, the scaled dual bound gives $|q_z(w)-c|\le Ch_K^{-1}\|w-c\|_{L^2(L_z)}$. The hat bounds and patch Poincaré argument in the proof of [F2] therefore give $\|w-Jw\|_{L^2(K)}\le Ch_K\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$ and $\|
abla Jw\|_{L^2(K)}\le C\|
abla w\|_{L^2(\omega_K)}$. Applying the same scaled trace inequality as in [F2] gives its edge bound as well. All these operations have input $w\in H_0^1(\Omega)$; shifted functions enter only the local integrals. [A1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $d=U_*-U$. The fine Galerkin equation and coarse equation imply $a(u-U_*,d)=0$ and $a(u-U,Jd)=0$. Since $b$ is constant and $d\in H_0^1(\Omega)$, $\int(b\cdot
abla d)d=0$, so $a(d,d)=\|
abla d\|_2^2$. Also $a(u-U,d)=a(d,d)$ because $u-U=d+(u-U_*)$ and fine orthogonality kills the latter term paired with $d$. Hence $\|
abla d\|_2^2=a(u-U,d-Jd)$. [A1, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 If $K
otin\mathcal R$, then $d$ is affine on $K$. At every interior vertex $z$ of $K$, the selected $L_z$ is also unchanged, so $d|_{L_z}$ is affine and its dual moment equals the common nodal value $d(z)$; boundary coefficients equal $d(z)=0$. Consequently $Jd=d$ on every unchanged cell. The trace of $d-Jd$ also vanishes on every edge incident to an unchanged cell. Thus [F1] applied to step 2.1 contains only volume residuals on $\mathcal R$ and interior edges with both incident cells in $\mathcal R$. Use the volume and edge estimates proved in step 1.1. The surviving squared residual weights are bounded by $C\sum_{K\in\mathcal R}\eta_K(U)^2$, since each surviving edge contribution occurs in the indicators of its incident refined cells. Cauchy–Schwarz and uniformly bounded overlap of the coarse vertex patches bound the other factor by $C\|
abla d\|_2$, giving $\|
abla d\|_2^2\le C\left(\sum_{K\in\mathcal R}\eta_K(U)^2ight)^{1/2}\|
abla d\|_2$. If this gradient norm is zero the claim is immediate; otherwise divide by it and square. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Fix a compatible labeled initial mesh. Recursive reference-edge closure of any finite marked set terminates, produces a matching conforming NVB descendant, and preserves the shape bound of [[lem-afem-nvb-shape-regularity-and-three-generation-properties]]. For a sequence of such refinements in which each selected cell is first requested for three uniform generations, there is a constant $C_{\rm cl}$ depending only on the initial mesh such that
$$\#\mathcal T_n-\#\mathcal T_0\le C_{\rm cl}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\#M_k.$$
The constant is for the cumulative sequence; no uniform bound on the added cells in one single refinement call is asserted.

1.1 For a current cell $K$, follow the neighbor across its reference edge while that edge is interior. If the neighbor is $L$, the common label is $g(K)$. By [F1], either $g(L)=g(K)$ and the pair is compatibly divisible, or $g(L)=g(K)-1$. In the second case continue from $L$. The generation is a nonnegative integer, so after finitely many strict drops the chain reaches the boundary or a compatible pair. To refine $K$, recursively refine this chain from its terminal end back to $K$. A terminal boundary cell is bisected first; a terminal compatible pair is bisected simultaneously. Inductively, the next cell in the chain has its reference edge on the edge just bisected, so that midpoint is already present on the other side when it is split. Thus every split matches its neighbor and conformity is preserved. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $g(K)$ denote generation. Each bisection halves area, and [F2] gives constants $c_0,C_0>0$ depending only on the finitely many initial shapes such that $c_0\,2^{-g(K)}\le |K|\le C_0\,2^{-g(K)}$ and $\operatorname{diam}K\le C_0\,2^{-g(K)/2}$. In the backward chain of step 1.1 there is at most one cell at each generation, plus at most one terminal compatible partner. Hence the sum of diameters from generation $g_{\min}$ upward is at most $D_0 2^{-g_{\min}/2}$ with $D_0=2C_0/(1-2^{-1/2})$. Every cell created while closing a request on $K$ is a child of a chain cell $L$ with $g(L)\le g(K)$, so its generation satisfies $g(T)=g(L)+1\le g(K)+1$. The portion of the chain between $K$ and $L$ has its lowest generation $g(L)$; summing its diameters gives $\operatorname{dist}(K,T)\le D_1 2^{-g(T)/2}$ with $D_1=2\sqrt2D_0$. The chain is finite by the integer generation drop, and these estimates supply the geometric radius used below. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 First consider one-generation requests in a finite sequence and let $\mathcal M$ be the union of all requested cells. For a final cell $T$ and marked cell $T^*$ define a nonnegative allocation $\lambda(T,T^*)=\begin{cases}a(g(T^*)-g(T)),& \operatorname{dist}(T,T^*)<D\,B\,2^{-g(T)/2}\ \text{and }g(T)\le g(T^*)+1,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}$ where $a(\ell)=(\ell+2)^{-2}$ for $\ell\ge-1$, $b(\ell)=2^{\ell/3}$ for $\ell\ge0$, $A=\sum_{\ell\ge-1}a(\ell)<\infty$, $B=\sum_{\ell\ge0}2^{-\ell/2}b(\ell)<\infty$, and $D=2D_1+2C_0$, with $D_1$ from step 2.1. The series for $B$ is geometric with ratio $2^{-1/6}<1$, and $c_*=\inf_{\ell\ge1}a(\ell)b(\ell)>0$ because $2^{\ell/3}/(\ell+2)^2$ tends to infinity. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

3.2 Fix $T^*\in\mathcal M$ with generation $g^*$. At a fixed generation $g\le g^*+1$, cells with nonzero allocation lie in a ball of radius $D B2^{-g/2}$ about $T^*$. Each has area at least $c_0 2^{-g}$ by step 2.1, while that ball enlarged by one cell diameter has area at most $C_D2^{-g}$. Since cell interiors are disjoint, their number is at most a constant $N_D$ independent of $g,T^*$, and the final level. Summing weights over generations therefore gives $\sum_{T\in\mathcal T_n\setminus\mathcal T_0}\lambda(T,T^*)\le N_D\sum_{\ell\ge-1}a(\ell)=N_DA=:C_1.$ [step 2.1, given, algebra]

3.3 Fix a new cell $T_0$ in the final forest. Trace its unique parent backward through the finite refinement history. If the parent was created during closure, take the least-ID requested cell whose recursive chain created it; repeat this at each earlier creation time. This gives a finite sequence of requested cells $T_1,\ldots,T_J$ ending at an initial cell. Step 2.1 gives $g(T_{j+1})\ge g(T_j)-1$ and, for each consecutive pair in the sequence, $\operatorname{dist}(T_{j-1},T_j)\le D_1 2^{-g(T_{j-1})/2}$. Let $s$ be the first index with $g(T_s)=g(T_0)-1$. The prefix whose links join $T_0$ to $T_s$ is $T_0,\ldots,T_{s-1}$; each of its generations is $g(T_0)+\ell$ for some $\ell\ge0$. The chain-distance estimate and the triangle inequality imply that if this prefix has at most $b(\ell)$ cells at every generation $g(T_0)+\ell$, then $\operatorname{dist}(T_0,T_s)\le D B\,2^{-g(T_0)/2}.$ Thus the terminal requested cell $T_s$ lies in the allocation radius and contributes $a(-1)>0$. Otherwise let $j_*$ be the first prefix with more than $b(\ell_*)$ cells at some generation $g(T_0)+\ell_*$. Every earlier link prefix satisfies the displayed distance bound. If $\ell_*=0$, since $T_0$ is new and $b(0)=1$, at least one other cell of that generation is a marked cell and contributes $a(0)$. If $\ell_*>0$, all cells of that generation in the prefix are marked; each lies within the allocation radius and contributes $a(\ell_*)$. In this case their total is greater than $a(\ell_*)b(\ell_*)\ge c_*$. Hence every new cell receives at least $C_2=\min\{a(-1),a(0),c_*\}>0$ allocation. [step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 Sum the lower bound from step 3.3 over new cells and interchange the two finite sums. The upper bound from step 3.2 gives $C_2(\#\mathcal T_n-\#\mathcal T_0)\le\sum_{T^*\in\mathcal M}\sum_{T\notin\mathcal T_0}\lambda(T,T^*)\le C_1\#\mathcal M.$ For three requested generations, view each marked parent as three successive one-generation requests. The number of virtual requests at generation stages $j=1,2,3$ is at most $2^{j-1}\#M_k$, since one bisection creates two children. Their total is at most $(1+2+4)\#M_k=7\#M_k$. Applying the one-generation estimate and summing over $k$ proves the claim with $C_{\rm cl}=7C_1/C_2$. [step 3.2, step 3.3, algebra] ∎

Inductively, the next cell in the chain has its reference edge on the edge just bisected, so that midpoint is already present on the other side when it is split. ## Statement

Let $\mathcal H_\ell$ be the degree-$\ell$ spaces on $\mathbb S^2$ from [[def-three-dimensional-spherical-harmonic-space]], with surface measure of total mass $4\pi$, and let $P_\ell$ be orthogonal projection in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$. Define $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$ by the polar-coordinate identity $\Delta=\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$. Then $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g=-\ell(\ell+1)g$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$; for all smooth $v,w$ on the sphere, $\langle v,\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}w\rangle=\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v,w\rangle$; the spaces are mutually orthogonal and their algebraic sum is uniformly dense in $C(\mathbb S^2;\mathbb C)$. For smooth $f$, for every integer $m\ge1$ there is a constant $C_m(f)$ such that $\|P_\ell f\|_2\le C_m(f)(1+\ell)^{-m}$. For $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$,
$$\|g\|_\infty\le\sqrt{\frac{2\ell+1}{4\pi}}\,\|g\|_2.$$
For each integer $p\ge0$ there is $C_p$ independent of $\ell,g$ such that $\|g\|_{C^p(\mathbb S^2)}\le C_p(1+\ell)^{p+1/2}\|g\|_2$.
The angular Dirichlet form satisfies $-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$ for $g\in\mathcal H_\ell$.
For every continuous $f$, the ordered partial sums $\sum_{\ell=0}^N P_\ell f$ converge to $f$ in $L^2(\mathbb S^2)$.

1.1 For a homogeneous polynomial $Q_n$ of degree $n$, direct differentiation and Euler's identity give $\Delta(|x|^{2j}Q_n)=2j(2n+2j+1)|x|^{2j-2}Q_n+|x|^{2j}\Delta Q_n$. For homogeneous $P$ of degree $n$, set $H=P+\sum_{j=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}a_j|x|^{2j}\Delta^jP$, where $a_0=1$ and $a_{j+1}=-a_j/[2(j+1)(2n-2j-1)]$. Substitution into the displayed identity makes the coefficient of each $|x|^{2j}\Delta^{j+1}P$ equal to $a_j+2(j+1)(2n-2j-1)a_{j+1}=0$; the last Laplacian power vanishes by degree. Thus $H$ is homogeneous harmonic and $P-H$ is divisible by $|x|^2$. Induction on degree shows that restrictions of polynomials are finite sums of elements of the spaces $\mathcal H_j$. [F1, algebra]

1.2 The polar-coordinate identity $\Delta=\partial_{rr}+2r^{-1}\partial_r+r^{-2}\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$ applied to $r^\ell Y(\omega)$, whose extension is harmonic by [F1], gives $\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}Y=-\ell(\ell+1)Y$. On the sphere, integration by parts gives $\langle v,\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}w\rangle=\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}v,w\rangle$: in $(\theta,\phi)$ coordinates integrate the $\phi$ derivative over its period and the $\theta$ term with weight $\sin\theta$; the pole boundary terms vanish because smooth functions and their spherical gradients are bounded while $\sin\theta\to0$. Distinct degrees have distinct eigenvalues, so their spaces are orthogonal. [F1, algebra]

1.3 Choose a finite orthonormal basis from [F2] and write $g=\sum_m c_mY_{\ell m}$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|g(\omega)|^2\le(\sum_m|c_m|^2)(\sum_m|Y_{\ell m}(\omega)|^2)$. Orthonormality identifies the first sum with $\|g\|_2^2$, and [F2] gives the second as $(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)$. Taking the supremum proves the evaluation bound. [F2, algebra]

2.1 Real polynomial restrictions contain constants and separate distinct points of $\mathbb S^2$ by a coordinate function. Compactness and [F3] make them dense in real $C(\mathbb S^2)$; applying this separately to real and imaginary parts gives density in complex $C(\mathbb S^2)$. By step 1.1 this is density of the algebraic sum of the $\mathcal H_j$. For continuous $f$ and $\varepsilon>0$, choose a finite sum $q$ of harmonic modes with $\|f-q\|_\infty<\varepsilon$. Put $P_{\le N}f=\sum_{\ell=0}^N P_\ell f$ and $V_N=\bigoplus_{\ell=0}^N\mathcal H_\ell$. Orthogonality from step 1.2 makes $f-P_{\le N}f$ orthogonal to $V_N$, so Pythagoras shows $P_{\le N}f$ is a best $L^2$ approximation in $V_N$. For $N$ at least the largest degree in $q$, $\|f-P_{\le N}f\|_2\le\|f-q\|_2\le\sqrt{4\pi}\varepsilon$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, the ordered partial sums converge in $L^2$. [F3, step 1.1, step 1.2, choose, algebra]

2.2 For smooth $f$ and $\ell\ge1$, self-adjointness just proved gives $P_\ell(\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}^m f)=(-\ell(\ell+1))^mP_\ell f$. The finite-dimensional projection is a contraction in $L^2$, hence $\|P_\ell f\|_2\le[\ell(\ell+1)]^{-m}\|\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}^m f\|_2$. Taking $m$ arbitrarily large proves the asserted decay (and degree zero is absorbed into $C_m(f)$). [step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Let $X_1,X_2,X_3$ be the infinitesimal rotation fields on the sphere about the coordinate axes. Rotations preserve $\mathcal H_\ell$ and surface measure, so $X_j$ preserves $\mathcal H_\ell$ and is skew-adjoint. Expanding these three fields in spherical coordinates gives $X_1^2+X_2^2+X_3^2=\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}$. Thus $\sum_j\|X_jg\|_2^2=-\langle\Delta_{\mathbb S^2}g,g\rangle=\ell(\ell+1)\|g\|_2^2$, so each $X_j$ has operator norm at most $\sqrt{\ell(\ell+1)}$ on $\mathcal H_\ell$. Iteration and step 1.3 bound every word of $q$ rotation derivatives pointwise by $\sqrt{(2\ell+1)/(4\pi)}[\ell(\ell+1)]^{q/2}\|g\|_2$. A finite smooth coordinate cover of the compact sphere expresses each coordinate derivative through order $p$ as bounded smooth combinations of words in the $X_j$ of order at most $p$; compactness supplies a finite cover by [F3], and absorbing its chart bounds gives the stated $C_p(1+\ell)^{p+1/2}$ estimate. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For a nondegenerate oriented triangle $K\subset\mathbb R^2$, set $R(a,b)=(-b,a)$, let $n$ be cell-outward and $t=Rn$. If $\sigma\in H(\operatorname{div};K)$ is real, then $R\sigma\in H(\operatorname{curl};K)$, $\operatorname{curl}(R\sigma)=\operatorname{div}\sigma$ distributionally, and $\int_K(R\sigma\cdot R\nabla\phi+\operatorname{curl}(R\sigma)\phi)=\langle\gamma_n\sigma,[\phi]\rangle$ for all $\phi\in H^1(K)$. Thus weak tangential trace equals weak normal trace under $t=Rn$.

Here $H(\operatorname{curl};K):=\{w\in L^2(K;\mathbb R^2):\partial_1w_2-\partial_2w_1\in L^2(K)\}$ with its graph norm. The weak tangential trace is the functional on $H^1(K)/H^1_0(K)$ defined by the integral in the Statement; the computation below proves it is the rotation of the PE08 weak normal trace.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and $d\ge2$. Let $A_t$ be the ALE moving-domain map of [[def-ale-moving-domain-map]], and let $g(x,t)$ and its first derivatives be continuous on the moving closure. Then, for each $t\in(0,T)$,

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\Omega(t)}g(x,t)\,dx=\int_{\Omega(t)}\partial_tg(x,t)\,dx+\int_{\partial\Omega(t)}g(x,t)w_m(x,t)\cdot n(x,t)\,dS.$$

Here $n$ is the outward normal from the transported finite piecewise-$C^1$ boundary presentation. This is a continuous transport identity; no discrete high-dimensional geometric conservation estimate follows from it.

## Statement

For every input satisfying [[alg-ale-upwind-finite-volume-step]], the procedure completes after finitely many operations and returns exactly one of `mesh_crossing` (with no updated state, if some $J_i^{n+1}\le0$) or `success` (with a unique updated array, if all $J_i^{n+1}>0$). Whenever it returns `success`, it preserves total periodic mass, $\sum_iJ_i^{n+1}\bar u_i^{n+1}=\sum_iJ_i^n\bar u_i^n$. It also preserves every constant state: if $\bar u_i^n=U$ for every cell, then $\bar u_i^{n+1}=U$ for every cell. The mass and constant-state properties require no CFL condition.

## Example

The Courant displacement is $b\Delta t/h=4.8$, so the backtracked foot crosses more than four cells. Give the two grid nodes bracketing that foot values $2$ and $10$.

1.1 Since $b=1$, the explicit Euler foot at $x_0=0$ is $-3/10$, which wraps to $7/10$ on the unit torus. On the lift, $(-3/10)/h=-24/5=-5+1/5$, so the lower index is $-5\equiv11\pmod{16}$, the upper index is $12$, and $\theta=1/5$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 The update is therefore $(1-\theta)2+\theta10=(4/5)2+(1/5)10=18/5$. By [F2] this value lies in $[2,10]$, despite the 4.8-cell displacement. The example uses no displacement CFL restriction. [given, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a nonzero finite open-boundary TT have order $d\ge2$, and choose a center window $[s,t]$ with $1\le s\le t\le d$ and $t-s+1\in\{1,2\}$. There is an exact rank-revealing QR transformation of its cores that preserves the represented array, makes every core $k<s$ left-isometric and every core $k>t$ right-isometric, and removes exactly the dependent coordinates on each swept bond. No independent column direction is truncated; only exactly dependent directions are removed.

For each reshaped matrix $M$, the rank-revealing QR used here scans its columns in their fixed order, retaining a column exactly when it increases the span. It applies Gram–Schmidt to the retained columns, writes all other columns in that orthonormal span, and records the resulting permutation and coefficient factor.

## Statement

For pair densities $f,g$ arising as finite products of Gaussian contractions in [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], let
$$\mathcal C(f,g)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\overline{f(x)}g(y)}{\|x-y\|_2}\,dy\,dx.$$
Then $\mathcal C$ is a well-defined Hermitian positive-semidefinite sesquilinear form on their finite linear span, and
$$|\mathcal C(f,g)|^2\le\mathcal C(f,f)\mathcal C(g,g).$$
For orbitals $\phi_a,\phi_b,\phi_c,\phi_d$ and pair densities $f_{ab}=\overline{\phi_a}\phi_b$, the integral convention in [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]] gives
$$|G(\phi_a,\phi_b;\phi_c,\phi_d)|\le\sqrt{G(\phi_a,\phi_b;\phi_a,\phi_b)G(\phi_c,\phi_d;\phi_c,\phi_d)},$$
where each diagonal quantity is nonnegative. For the real finite energy functional in [[def-finite-gaussian-basis-variational-energy-and-gradient]], let $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}$, $D\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$, and define the input-basis density coefficients $W_{ab}=\sum_{p,q=1}^r C_{ap}D_{pq}C_{bq}$. Here the $n$ input basis functions may themselves be contractions; a primitive basis is the singleton-contraction special case. Reindexing the finite two-body energy gives $E_2=\tfrac12\sum_{a,b,c,d}W_{ab}W_{cd}G_{ab,cd}$. Thus for any finite set $S$ of input-basis quartets omitted from that contraction,
$$B_S=\frac12\sum_{(a,b,c,d)\in S}|W_{ab}W_{cd}|\sqrt{G_{ab,ab}G_{cd,cd}}$$
is an accumulated upper bound for the absolute omitted energy contribution. This does not assert that a screened integral is zero.

1.1 For $r>0$, substitute $u=sr$ in the Gaussian integral [F3] and use symmetry to get $$\frac1r=\frac2{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-s^2r^2}\,ds.$$ The diagonal $x=y$ has product measure zero, and [F2] makes the integral of the absolute Coulomb integrand finite. Tonelli [F5] applied to its absolute value therefore permits the Laplace representation to be inserted into $\mathcal C(f,f)$. [given, F2, F3, F4, F5, algebra]

1.2 For fixed $s\ge0$, factor $$e^{-s^2\|x-y\|^2}=e^{-s^2\|x\|^2}e^{-s^2\|y\|^2}\prod_{j=1}^3e^{2s^2x_jy_j}.$$ Expanding the three exponentials gives a sum over $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$ with terms $(2s^2)^{|\alpha|}x^\alpha y^\alpha/\alpha!$. Its absolute sum after multiplying the Gaussian factors is at most one, because $\sum_j|x_jy_j|\le\|x\|\|y\|$ by [F6] and $\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2-2\|x\|\|y\|=(\|x\|-\|y\|)^2\ge0$. Since $f\in L^1$, Fubini [F5] interchanges this absolutely summable expansion with both integrals, yielding $$\int\int\overline{f(x)}f(y)e^{-s^2\|x-y\|^2}\,dy\,dx=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3}\frac{(2s^2)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\left|\int f(x)x^\alpha e^{-s^2\|x\|^2}\,dx\right|^2\ge0.$$ [given, F2, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 Integrating the nonnegative quantity in step 1.2 over $s$ with the factor $2/\sqrt\pi$ from step 1.1 gives $\mathcal C(f,f)\ge0$. Absolute convergence [F2] also makes $\mathcal C$ Hermitian and sesquilinear. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F2, algebra]

3.1 For $\mathcal C(g,g)>0$, expand $0\le\mathcal C(f+zg,f+zg)$ for arbitrary $z\in\mathbb C$ and choose $z=-\mathcal C(g,f)/\mathcal C(g,g)$; the resulting quadratic inequality is $|\mathcal C(f,g)|^2\le\mathcal C(f,f)\mathcal C(g,g)$. If $\mathcal C(g,g)=0$, the same nonnegative quadratic for all arbitrarily small $z$ forces its linear term to vanish, so $\mathcal C(f,g)=0$ and the inequality still holds. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By [F1], each two-electron entry is $\mathcal C(f_{ab},f_{cd})$. Applying step 3.1 gives its diagonal Cauchy–Schwarz bound and nonnegative diagonals. Substitute the four $C$ factors from [F7] into the finite two-body energy and reorder its finite sums; the coefficient of $G_{ab,cd}$ is $W_{ab}W_{cd}$. The absolute omitted contribution is at most the sum of the absolute values of its weighted terms, giving $B_S$. The sum is retained in the report, so no omitted entry is called exactly zero. [given, F1, F7, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the data of [[def-linear-elasticity-displacement-formulation-and-data]]. For every finite $\lambda\ge0$ there is a unique $u\in V$ such that $\mathcal E_\lambda(u,v)=f(v)$ for every $v\in V$. It satisfies
$$
\|u\|_V\le\mu_0^{-1}\|f\|_{V'},\qquad \sqrt{\mathcal E_\lambda(u,u)}\le\mu_0^{-1/2}\|f\|_{V'}.
$$
For every finite-dimensional conforming subspace $V_h\subset V$, the Galerkin solution $u_h$ is unique and
$$
\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac{2\mu_1+d\lambda}{\mu_0}\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.
$$

## Statement

Let $\mathcal T_h$ be a finite periodic matching affine simplicial mesh in $d\ge2$, let $\beta\in\mathbb R^d$ be constant, and apply [[alg-pe04-first-order-upwind-forward-euler]] with $\lambda_K\le1$ for every cell. Assume Countable Choice for the imported affine-simplex Green formula. Then the cell-volume-weighted mean is conserved:
$$\sum_KV_KU_K^+=\sum_KV_KU_K.$$
For every convex function $\eta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, the weighted discrete entropy does not increase:
$$\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K^+)\le\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K).$$

1.1 By [F2] with the constant vector field $\beta$, $\sum_FA_Fb_{K,F}=0$, hence $\sum_FA_F(-b_{K,F})^+=\sum_FA_Fb_{K,F}^+$. Rewriting [F1] gives $U_K^+=(1-\lambda_K)U_K+\sum_{F\subset\partial K}\frac{\Delta tA_F(-b_{K,F})^+}{V_K}U_{K_F}$. All coefficients are nonnegative by $\lambda_K\le1$, and their sum is $(1-\lambda_K)+\lambda_K=1$. [F1, F2, A1, algebra]

2.1 Convexity of $\eta$ and the convex-combination formula in step 1.1 give $V_K\eta(U_K^+)\le V_K(1-\lambda_K)\eta(U_K)+\Delta t\sum_FA_F(-b_{K,F})^+\eta(U_{K_F})$. Sum over cells. Each incoming coefficient for an upwind cell $J$ is paired with the equal outgoing coefficient $\Delta tA_Fb_{J,F}^+$ on that same periodic face, so these terms exactly fill the subtracted $V_J\lambda_J\eta(U_J)$ contributions. Therefore $\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K^+)\le\sum_KV_K\eta(U_K)$. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Multiply the update [F1] by $V_K$ and sum over cells. Every periodic interior face contributes one shared flux with each of its two opposite outward normals, so its two signed contributions cancel. This proves $\sum_KV_KU_K^+=\sum_KV_KU_K$. [F1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded connected polyhedral set and let $(\mathcal T_h)$ be a refining, uniformly regular, boundary-anchored family of TPFA-admissible meshes. Assume $\lambda_K\in[\lambda_*,\lambda^*]$ with $0<\lambda_*\le\lambda^*<\infty$, constant on each cell, and that coefficient jumps occur only across mesh faces. Suppose $u$ is continuous, vanishes on $\partial\Omega$, and is $C^2$ on each cell closure with the uniform family bound
$$ M=\sup_h\max_{K\in\mathcal K_h}\|D^2u\|_{L^\infty(K)}<\infty. $$
For every interior face $F=K|L$ fix an orientation and define its exact outward flux from $K$ by $J_{K,F}=-\int_F\lambda_K\nabla u|_K\cdot n_{K,F}$. On a boundary face define $J_{K,F}$ by the same formula. Assume the exact fluxes satisfy the cell balances $\sum_{F\subset\partial K}J_{K,F}=\int_K f$ and $J_{K,F}=-J_{L,F}$ on every interior face. Let $U_h$ solve the TPFA cell balances with source $f$ and zero boundary values, and let $I_hu$ be the cell-center sample $u(x_K)$ with zero boundary face values. Then, for a constant $C$ depending only on $\Omega$, $\lambda_*,\lambda^*$, and the uniform mesh regularity bounds,
$$ \|U_h-I_hu\|_{E_h}\le C hM,\qquad \left(\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_{\rm int}}\frac{|Q_{K,F}(U_h)-J_{K,F}|^2}{T_F}+\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_{\rm bdy}}\frac{|Q_{K,F}(U_h)-J_{K,F}|^2}{T_{K,F}}\right)^{1/2}\le 2ChM. $$
The second estimate is convergence of the reconstructed numerical face flux in the transmissibility-dual energy norm. No pointwise operator consistency on arbitrary nonorthogonal meshes or error rate for nonsmooth weak solutions is asserted.

For every interior face $F=K|L$ fix an orientation and define its exact outward flux from $K$ by $J_{K,F}=-\int_F\lambda_K\nabla u|_K\cdot n_{K,F}$. On a boundary face define $J_{K,F}$ by the same formula. Assume the exact fluxes satisfy the cell balances $\sum_{F\subset\partial K}J_{K,F}=\int_K f$ and $J_{K,F}=-J_{L,F}$ on every interior face. Let $U_h$ solve the TPFA cell balances with source $f$ and zero boundary values, and let $I_hu$ be the cell-center sample $u(x_K)$ with zero boundary face values. Then, for a constant $C$ depending only on $\Omega$, $\lambda_*,\lambda^*$, and the uniform mesh regularity bounds,
$$ \|U_h-I_hu\|_{E_h}\le C hM,\qquad \left(\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_{\rm int}}\frac{|Q_{K,F}(U_h)-J_{K,F}|^2}{T_F}+\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_{\rm bdy}}\frac{|Q_{K,F}(U_h)-J_{K,F}|^2}{T_{K,F}}\right)^{1/2}\le 2ChM. $$
The second estimate is convergence of the reconstructed numerical face flux in the transmissibility-dual energy norm. No pointwise operator consistency on arbitrary nonorthogonal meshes or error rate for nonsmooth weak solutions is asserted.

1.1 For each face orient the exact flux $J_F$ outward from one incident cell, and set $\delta_F=Q_{K,F}(I_hu)-J_F$; on a boundary face set $\delta_F=Q_{K,F}(I_hu)-J_{K,F}$. Let $y_F$ be the intersection of the center-normal line with an interior face and the orthogonal projection point on a boundary face. Taylor's theorem along the normal gives, on $F=K|L$ with $n=n_{K,F}$, $u(x_K)=u(y_F)-d_{K,F}\partial_nu_K(y_F)+r_K,\quad u(x_L)=u(y_F)+d_{L,F}\partial_nu_L(y_F)+r_L,$ where $|r_K|+|r_L|\le C M h^2$. By [A1], $\lambda_K\partial_nu_K(y_F)=\lambda_L\partial_nu_L(y_F)=s_F$. Substitution into the harmonic formula gives $Q_{K,F}(I_hu)=-|F|s_F+T_F(r_K-r_L)$. The face trace varies by at most $M h$ from $y_F$, so $|J_{K,F}+|F|s_F|\le C\lambda^*M|F|h$. Since [F1]–[F2] imply $T_F\le C|F|/h$, we obtain $|\delta_F|\le C M|F|h$. On a boundary face, $u(y_F)=0$ and the one-sided Taylor expansion $u(x_K)=-d_{K,F}\partial_nu_K(y_F)+r_K$ yields the same bound for $\delta_F$. [F1, F2, A1, given, algebra]

2.1 By uniform regularity, every transmissibility satisfies $T_F\ge c|F|/h$. There are at most $N_0$ faces per cell, $|F|\le Ch^{d-1}$, and $|K|\ge ch^d$, so $\#\mathcal K_h\le |\Omega|/(ch^d)$ and $\sum_F|F|\le C h^{-1}$. Step 1.1 therefore gives $\sum_F\frac{\delta_F^2}{T_F}\le C M^2h^3\sum_F|F|\le C M^2h^2.$ Thus the vector of local flux defects has transmissibility-dual norm at most $C hM$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Let $e=U_h-I_hu$. The exact cell balances in [A1] and the finite-volume balances for $U_h$ imply, for every cell vector $v$, $a_h(e,v)=-\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_{\rm int}}\delta_F(v_K-v_L)-\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_{\rm bdy}}\delta_Fv_K,$ because the two exact interior fluxes are oppositely oriented. 4.1 On every face, $Q_{K,F}(U_h)-Q_{K,F}(I_hu)$ equals $T_F(e_K-e_L)$ for an interior face and $T_{K,F}e_K$ for a boundary face. Its transmissibility-dual norm is therefore exactly $\|e\|_{E_h}$. By the triangle inequality, the numerical-flux error norm is at most $\|e\|_{E_h}+(\sum_F\delta_F^2/T_F)^{1/2}\le2ChM$, using steps 2.1 and 3.1. This proves both estimates. [F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $d\in\{2,3\}$, $\Omega=(0,1)^d$, and let
$M\ge2$ and $n\ge2$ be integers. Write $e_1,\ldots,e_d$ for the standard
coordinate vectors in $\mathbb R^d$. In every cube of side $a=1/M$, for each
coordinate permutation $\pi$ use the simplex whose successive vertices,
with $x$ the cube's lower corner, are
$x$, $x+a e_{\pi(1)}$, $x+a(e_{\pi(1)}+e_{\pi(2)})$, through
$x+a\sum_{r=1}^d e_{\pi(r)}$. Subdivide each cube into $n^d$ uniform fine
cubes and apply the same permutation rule at fine scale; this gives nested,
matching, shape-regular affine simplicial meshes
$\mathcal T_H\subset\mathcal T_h$. Write $H=\sqrt d\,a$ and
$h=\sqrt d\,a/n$. Assume an overlap radius $\delta=q a/n$ with integer
$\lceil\sqrt d\rceil\le q\le n$, so $h\le\delta\le a$. For each
coarse cube $Q_j$, let $\Omega_j$ be its closed $\ell^\infty$-neighborhood of
radius $\delta+h$, intersected with $\overline\Omega$. Let $V_H\subset V_h
\subset H_0^1(\Omega)$ be the continuous zero-boundary P1 spaces on the
coarse and fine meshes, and let
$$ V_j=\{v_h\in V_h:\operatorname{supp}v_h\subseteq\Omega_j\}. $$
Here $\|x\|_\infty=\max_r|x_r|$,
$\operatorname{dist}_\infty(x,Q)=\inf_{y\in Q}\|x-y\|_\infty$, an
$\ell^\infty$-neighborhood of radius $r$ is
$\{x:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(x,Q)\le r\}$, and $\operatorname{supp}v$ is
the closure in $\overline\Omega$ of $\{x:v(x)\ne0\}$.
For the Poisson energy $a(u,v)=\int_\Omega\nabla u\cdot\nabla v\,dx$, every
$u_h\in V_h$ has a decomposition $u_h=u_0+\sum_j u_j$ with
$u_0\in V_H$ and $u_j\in V_j$ satisfying
$$ a(u_0,u_0)+\sum_j a(u_j,u_j) \le C_{\rm FE}\left(1+\left(\frac H\delta\right)^2\right)a(u_h,u_h). $$
The constant $C_{\rm FE}$ depends only on $d$, the fixed uniform
shape-regularity bound, the Scott–Zhang constant, and the reference P1 product
interpolation constants; it is independent of $M,n,\delta$.

Assume Countable Choice and the nonempty mesh hypotheses of [[def-nitsche-boundary-penalty-forms]]. Let $N_\partial$ be the maximum number of boundary facets incident to a single cell, and use the selected positive local constant $C_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge1$ from [[lem-nitsche-local-polynomial-flux-inverse-trace]]. The mesh has at least one boundary facet, so $1\le N_\partial\le d+1$ and $C_\partial:=\sqrt{N_\partial}C_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge1$. For every $v_h\in V_h$,
$$\left(\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}h_F\|\partial_n v_h\|_{L^2(F)}^2\right)^{1/2}\le C_\partial\|\nabla v_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)},\qquad C_\partial:=\sqrt{N_\partial}\,C_{\mathrm{tr}}.$$
Consequently,
$$\left|\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}\int_F(\partial_n v_h)v_h\,dS\right|\le C_\partial\|\nabla v_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\left(\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_h^\partial}h_F^{-1}\|v_h\|_{L^2(F)}^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
For simplices $N_\partial\le d+1$; no sharper face-count bound is needed.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. For every $\lambda\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$, with $\Gamma$ as in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]], there is a unique $u=S\lambda\in\dot H^1(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying the weak single-layer equation of [[def-bem-laplace-layer-potentials-and-energy-spaces]]. It is harmonic on $\Omega^-$ and $\Omega^+$, its two traces agree, and its weak conormal traces satisfy
$$\partial_n^-u-\partial_n^+u=\lambda\quad\hbox{in }H^{-1/2}(\Gamma).$$
The trace operator $V\lambda:=\gamma u$ maps $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ boundedly into $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, and there are constants $C,c>0$ depending on $\Gamma$ such that
$$\|u\|_{\dot H^1}+\|V\lambda\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}},\qquad \langle\lambda,V\lambda\rangle_\Gamma\ge c\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}^2.$$
If $\lambda\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ (in particular for facewise smooth densities reaching edges or discontinuous P0 densities), this weak potential agrees away from $\Gamma$ with $\int_\Gamma(4\pi|x-y|)^{-1}\lambda(y)dS_y$.

1.1 For fixed $\lambda$, define $\ell(v)=\langle\lambda,\gamma v\rangle_\Gamma$ on $\dot H^1$. The trace estimate in [F1] gives $|\ell(v)|\le C\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}\|v\|_{\dot H^1}$. The gradient inner product makes $\dot H^1$ a real Hilbert space by its completion definition, so [F2] applied to $a(u,v)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v$ gives a unique $u$ with $a(u,v)=\ell(v)$ for every $v$, and $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\le C\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}$. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

2.1 Testing with smooth functions compactly supported off $\Gamma$ makes the right side zero, so $u$ is weakly harmonic in each side. The same weak equation for a global smooth test $v$ is the distributional identity $-\Delta u=\lambda\delta_\Gamma$, where $\langle\lambda\delta_\Gamma,v\rangle=\langle\lambda,\gamma v\rangle_\Gamma$. Splitting the energy integral across $\Omega^-$ and $\Omega^+$ and using the weak Green definitions in [[def-bem-laplace-layer-potentials-and-energy-spaces]] gives $\langle\partial_n^-u-\partial_n^+u,\gamma v\rangle=\langle\lambda,\gamma v\rangle$; the right inverse in [F1] makes every $H^{1/2}$ trace available, hence the conormal jump is $\lambda$. The global $\dot H^1$ representative has one trace, so $\gamma^-u=\gamma^+u=\gamma u$. [F1, F3, step 1.1, given]

3.1 By the weak equation tested with $v=u$, $\langle\lambda,V\lambda\rangle=\|u\|_{\dot H^1}^2$. For any $g\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ with $\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}\le1$, choose the bounded lift $Lg$ from [F1]; then $|\langle\lambda,g\rangle|=|\int\nabla u\cdot\nabla Lg|\le C\|u\|_{\dot H^1}$. Taking the supremum over such $g$ gives $\|\lambda\|_{H^{-1/2}}\le C\|u\|_{\dot H^1}$. Combining this with the energy identity proves coercivity; applying the trace bound of [F1] and the estimate in step 1.1 proves boundedness of $V$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Now let $\lambda\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$, and put $U(x)=\int_\Gamma G_3(x,y)\lambda(y)dS_y$. Such a density belongs to $H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ because $|\int_\Gamma\lambda g|\le\|\lambda\|_2\|g\|_2\le C\|\lambda\|_2\|g\|_{H^{1/2}}$. The finite number of planar faces gives $|\Gamma\cap B(x,r)|\le Cr^2$ for small $r$. Dyadic annuli about $x$ therefore bound $|U(x)|$ locally by $C$ and $|
abla U(x)|$ by $C(1+|\log d(x,\Gamma)|)$: on each annulus of radius $r$, the kernels $|x-y|^{-1}$ and $|x-y|^{-2}$ contribute at most $Cr$ and $C$, respectively, and there are at most $C(1+|\log d|)$ annuli. A width-$\delta$ neighborhood of a finite union of planar polygons has volume at most $C\delta$ (each face contributes a prism of volume $O(\delta)$, each edge a tube of volume $O(\delta^2)$, and each vertex a ball of volume $O(\delta^3)$). Summing dyadic distance strips shows $
abla U\in L^2$ near $\Gamma$; at infinity $U=O(|x|^{-1})$ and $
abla U=O(|x|^{-2})$. The displayed gradient is also the global weak gradient: the first derivative of the locally integrable Newton kernel is locally volume integrable, so the weak derivative of its surface convolution is the same integral by Fubini. Hence $U\in L^6$ and $
abla U\in L^2$. To see that $U$ belongs to the completion $\dot H^1$, take cutoffs $\chi_R=1$ on $B_R$, supported in $B_{2R}$, with $|
abla\chi_R|\le C/R$: the gradient tail tends to zero and $R^{-2}\int_{R<|x|<2R}|U|^2=O(R^{-1})$. Each $\chi_RU$ is compactly supported in $H^1$ and convolution approximates it in $H^1$ by smooth compactly supported functions. The fundamental-solution identity [F3] and Fubini [F4], whose local absolute-integrability follows from $|
abla_xG_3|=O(|x-y|^{-2})$ in three dimensions, give $\int
abla U\cdot
abla v=\int_\Gamma\lambda\gamma v$ for smooth compactly supported $v$. Density and [F1] extend this to all $v\in\dot H^1$. Uniqueness in step 1.1 gives $U=u$, proving the kernel representation. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $F\in C^1$ and let $y_*\in\mathbb R^2$ be a homogeneous equilibrium, $F(y_*)=0$. Set $J=DF(y_*)=(J_{ij})$, assume $\operatorname{tr}J<0$ and $\det J>0$, and let $D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,d_2)$ with $d_1,d_2>0$. For any spatial eigenfunction of $-\Delta$ with eigenvalue $\lambda\ge0$, the linearized reaction-diffusion mode has matrix $J-\lambda D$. For the continuous rectangular torus, $\lambda=\lambda_k=\sum_j(2\pi k_j/L_j)^2$ with $k\in\mathbb Z^d$. For the periodic grid of [[def-periodic-reaction-diffusion-grid]], the mode indexed by $\ell$ has $\lambda=\lambda_{h,\ell}=4\sum_jh_j^{-2}\sin^2(\pi\ell_j/N_j)$, with $0\le\ell_j<N_j$.

Define
$$
\beta_T=d_2J_{11}+d_1J_{22},\qquad q(\lambda)=\det(J-\lambda D)=d_1d_2\lambda^2-\beta_T\lambda+\det J.
$$
For either domain or grid and each actual mode, $J-\lambda D$ has a positive-real-part eigenvalue exactly when $q(\lambda)<0$; it is Hurwitz exactly when $q(\lambda)>0$, and has a zero eigenvalue when $q(\lambda)=0$. Thus the continuous or discrete linear instability criterion tests the actual corresponding spectrum. If all nonnegative $\lambda$ are regarded as continuously available, then a diffusion-driven unstable band exists exactly when $\beta_T>0$ and $\beta_T^2>4d_1d_2\det J$; its endpoints are
$$
\lambda_\pm=\frac{\beta_T\pm\sqrt{\beta_T^2-4d_1d_2\det J}}{2d_1d_2}.
$$
On a bounded torus or a finite grid, the band criterion alone is not enough: at least one actual Laplacian eigenvalue must lie strictly between $\lambda_-$ and $\lambda_+$.

2.2 The characteristic polynomial of a real $2\times2$ matrix $A$ is $\mu^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)\mu+\det(A)$. If $\operatorname{tr}(A)<0$ and $\det(A)<0$, its discriminant $\operatorname{tr}(A)^2-4\det(A)$ is positive and the real roots have negative product, so one is positive. If $\operatorname{tr}(A)<0$ and $\det(A)>0$, real roots have negative sum and positive product, so both are negative; nonreal roots are conjugate with real part $\operatorname{tr}(A)/2<0$. If the determinant is zero, one eigenvalue is zero and the other is the trace, which is negative. Applying these alternatives to $A=J-\lambda D$ proves the mode tests in the Statement. [step 1.2, algebra]

1.1 Write $u=y_*+\varepsilon w$. Differentiability of $F$ gives $F(y_*+\varepsilon w)=F(y_*)+\varepsilon Jw+o(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon Jw+o(\varepsilon)$, so the linearized equation is $w_t=D\Delta w+Jw$. For a continuous torus mode $w(t,x)=a(t)e^{2\pi i\sum_jk_jx_j/L_j}$, direct differentiation gives $\Delta w=-\lambda_kw$ and hence $a'=(J-\lambda_kD)a$. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 For the grid, insert a Fourier vector from [F3] into the linearized finite system. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $Q=(0,1)^d$, $d\in\{2,3\}$. Use a common finite tensor-product B-spline basis $N_\alpha$ of coordinate degrees $p_r\ge1$, clamped endpoint multiplicities $p_r+1$, and interior multiplicities at most $p_r$. Only positive-length knot spans are cells. Exact homogeneous re-representation on this common basis must be established before comparing data on originally different grids; it is not inferred from a common geometric image. Let
$$A=\sum_\alpha a_\alpha N_\alpha,\quad W=\sum_\alpha w_\alpha N_\alpha,\quad F=A/W,\qquad A'=\sum_\alpha a'_\alpha N_\alpha,\quad W'=\sum_\alpha w'_\alpha N_\alpha,\quad G=A'/W'.$$
Here $a_\alpha=w_\alpha P_\alpha\in\mathbb R^d$ and $a'_\alpha=w'_\alpha P'_\alpha$. Suppose $F$ is admissible in [[def-nurbs-patch-map-and-rational-spline-space]], $w_-\le w_\alpha\le w_+$, $\|DF\|,\|(DF)^{-1}\|\le L$, $\det DF\ge j_->0$, and the global lower Lipschitz bound is explicitly $|F(x)-F(y)|\ge c|x-y|$ on $\overline Q$, $c>0$. The latter is the reciprocal of a global inverse Lipschitz bound and need not equal $1/L$.

Define finite data quantities
$$\epsilon_A=\max_\alpha|a'_\alpha-a_\alpha|,\quad \epsilon_W=\max_\alpha|w'_\alpha-w_\alpha|<w_-,\quad m=w_--\epsilon_W>0,\quad R=\max_\alpha|P_\alpha|,$$
$$H=\sum_\alpha\max_C\|\nabla N_\alpha\|_{L^\infty(C)},\quad T=\epsilon_A+R\epsilon_W,\qquad E_0=T/m,$$
$$E_1=\frac{H\epsilon_A+L\epsilon_W+RH\epsilon_W}{m}+\frac{T(w_++\epsilon_W)H}{m^2}.$$
All vector norms are Euclidean and all derivative norms are operator norms. $H$ is defined by the actual cell polynomials, so retains every degree, knot-spacing and multiplicity dependence. It is finite on each fixed finite nondegenerate grid; no uniform bound over degenerating grids is asserted. Then $w'_\alpha\ge m$, $G$ is continuous on $\overline Q$, and
$$e_0:=\|F-G\|_\infty\le E_0,\qquad e_1:=\|DF-DG\|_{L^\infty(\text{cells};op)}\le E_1.$$
If $E_1<\min(c,1/L)$, then $G$ is globally injective and bi-Lipschitz onto its image, and
$$|G(x)-G(y)|\ge(c-E_1)|x-y|,\quad \|DG\|\le L+E_1,\quad \|(DG)^{-1}\|\le\frac{L}{1-LE_1},\quad \det DG\ge j_-(1-LE_1)^d>0.$$
The image $G(Q)$ is open. For the admissible-patch conclusion, retain the explicit boundary hypothesis that $G(Q)$ is a Lipschitz domain with its finite piecewise $C^1$ knot-cell presentation. A sufficient verifiable alternative is that $G$ extends $C^1$ to a neighborhood of $\overline Q$ with nonsingular derivative there; this alternative holds when every interior multiplicity is at most $p_r-1$. With either boundary condition $G$ is admissible. No equality of the physical boundaries of $F(Q)$ and $G(Q)$ is asserted; their correspondence is $G\circ F^{-1}$.

For these admissible maps put
$$M=\max\left(1,L,L+E_1,\frac{L}{1-LE_1}\right),\qquad C_M=dM^{d+1}+2M^{d+3}.$$
Their unit-Laplace tensors satisfy $\|K_F-K_G\|_\infty\le C_ME_1$, and their bilinear-form difference is at most $C_ME_1\|\nabla v\|_2\|\nabla w\|_2$. For any family with uniformly bounded $L,c^{-1},R,w_+,m^{-1}$ and $H\epsilon_A+H\epsilon_W+\epsilon_W=O(h^s)$, $s>0$, the geometry form defect is $O(h^s)$. The bound is generated from homogeneous data; convergence of those data remains a separate approximation or certification obligation. Loads, quadrature and boundary-lift defects remain separate.

A concrete geometry generator is scalar rounding of every component of $a_\alpha$ and every $w_\alpha$ to the nearest multiple of $2^{-b}$ (ties go to the smaller integer), followed by $P'_\alpha=a'_\alpha/w'_\alpha$. Put $\eta_b=2^{-b-1}$ and
$$D=\frac{2H\sqrt d+2L+2RH}{w_-}+\frac{4(\sqrt d+R)(w_++w_-/2)H}{w_-^2}.$$
Choose an integer $b\ge0$ such that $\eta_b<\min(w_-/2,c/(2D),1/(2LD))$. Then this generator has $\epsilon_A\le\sqrt d\,\eta_b$, $\epsilon_W\le\eta_b$, $e_0\le2(\sqrt d+R)\eta_b/w_-$, and $e_1\le D\eta_b$; in particular it generates the positive denominator, Jacobian, and global injectivity bounds above. In the $C^1$ knot branch ($\mu_r\le p_r-1$) it generates admissible approximate domains without an independent boundary certificate. Taking $b$ so that $D\eta_b\le h^s$ produces a stated geometry derivative rate for any supplied grid family, with its actual $D$, rather than claiming a rate from positive weights or knot refinement alone.

## Statement

Assume the hypotheses of [[thm-meshfree-particle-kernel-quadrature-error]] and let f∈C³(R^d) have bounded derivatives. There are constants C₀,C₁, independent of ε,h and the interior point x, such that

$$|Q^0_{\varepsilon,h}f(x)-f(x)|\le C_0\varepsilon^2\|D^2f\|_\infty+C_1h\bigl(\|\nabla f\|_\infty+\varepsilon^{-1}\|f\|_\infty\bigr),$$

$$|Q^1_{\varepsilon,h}f(x)-\nabla f(x)|\le C_0\varepsilon^2\|D^3f\|_\infty+C_1h\bigl(\varepsilon^{-1}\|\nabla f\|_\infty+\varepsilon^{-2}\|f\|_\infty\bigr).$$

## Definition

Let $\mathcal I=\{1,\ldots,M\}$ be a nonempty finite periodic node set. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ be diagonal with strictly positive entries, and for each direction $j=1,\ldots,d$ let $D_j\in\mathbb R^{M\times M}$ satisfy the periodic diagonal-norm SBP identities

$$HD_j+D_j^TH=0,\qquad D_j\mathbf1=0.$$

For a nodal array $w=(w_i)_{i\in\mathcal I}$, $D_jw$ means componentwise matrix multiplication, $(D_jw)_i=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal I}(D_j)_{i\ell}w_\ell$. Given admissible nodal states $U_i\in\mathcal G$, write $v_i=v(U_i)$. Define the semidiscrete system

$$\dot U_i+2\sum_{j=1}^d\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal I}(D_j)_{i\ell}F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}(U_i,U_\ell) =\sum_{j,k=1}^d\left[D_j\left(\bigl(K_{jk}(U_i)(D_kv)_i\bigr)_{i\in\mathcal I}\right)\right]_i, \qquad i\in\mathcal I,$$

where $F_j^{\mathrm{ec}}$ is the two-point flux in [[def-ideal-gas-entropy-conservative-pair-flux]] and $K_{jk}$ is the viscous block matrix in [[lem-compressible-viscous-flux-entropy-variable-factorization]]. This definition specifies a periodic semidiscrete operator on $\mathcal G^M$; it does not include a time discretization or a positivity limiter.

1.1 Under `(stay, exit)`, the policy equations are $V_0=0$ and $V_1=2$, so $V=(0,2)$. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Gaussian probability law.
Let $A\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ be fixed, let $k\ge2$, $p\ge2$ be integers
with $\ell=k+p\le\min(m,n)$, and draw $\Omega\in\mathbb C^{n\times\ell}$
with iid normalized complex Gaussian entries satisfying $\mathbb E|g|^2=1$.
Let $Q$ be the exact finite-scan range-finder basis of
$\operatorname{Ran}(A\Omega)$ returned by
[[alg-gaussian-randomized-range-finder]], and put $P=QQ^*$. Then
$$\mathbb E\|(I-P)A\|_2\le\sqrt{\frac{\ell}{p}}\,\sigma_{k+1} +\frac{e\sqrt\ell}{p}\left(\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2\right)^{1/2}.$$
In particular, the original approved bound with leading coefficient
$1+\sqrt{k/(p-1)}$ follows. The algorithm and sketch width $\ell$ are
unchanged; only the analysis may use a larger SVD partition rank.

1.1 Choose an SVD $A=U\Sigma V^*$ and fix any deterministic analysis rank $a$ with $1\le a<\ell$. Write $V^*\Omega=[\Omega_1^T\ \Omega_2^T]^T$ with the first $a$ rows in $\Omega_1$. By [F2] these blocks are independent normalized complex Gaussian matrices, and by [F3] $\Omega_1$ has full row rank almost surely. In SVD coordinates set $Y=\Sigma V^*\Omega$ and $C_0=Y\Omega_1^\dagger[I_a\ 0]$; then $\operatorname{Ran}(C_0)\subseteq\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$. Since $\Omega_1\Omega_1^\dagger=I_a$, the first $a$ rows of $\Sigma-C_0$ vanish and its remaining rows are $[-T\ \ W]$, where $T=\Sigma_{>a}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger$ and $W=\Sigma_{>a}$. For the projector $\widetilde P$ onto $\operatorname{Ran}(Y)$, $(I-\widetilde P)C_0=0$. For any vector $z$, the two terms in $z=\widetilde Pz+(I-\widetilde P)z$ are orthogonal, so $\|(I-\widetilde P)z\|_2\le\|z\|_2$; taking the unit-vector supremum shows that this projector is contractive. Thus $\|(I-\widetilde P)\Sigma\|_2^2\le\|[-T\ \ W]\|_2^2$. The block identity $[-T\ \ W][-T\ \ W]^*=TT^*+WW^*$ and [F5] give $\|[-T\ \ W]\|_2^2=\|TT^*+WW^*\|_2$. The operator-norm triangle inequality follows by applying the vector triangle inequality to each unit vector and taking the supremum; the SVD gives $\|TT^*\|_2=\|T\|_2^2$ and $\|WW^*\|_2=\|W\|_2^2$. Hence $\|[-T\ \ W]\|_2^2\le\|T\|_2^2+\|W\|_2^2 =\|\Sigma_{>a}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2^2+\sigma_{a+1}^2$. Unitary invariance transfers this to $E^2\le\sigma_{a+1}^2+ \|\Sigma_{>a}\Omega_2\Omega_1^\dagger\|_2^2$, where $E=\|(I-P)A\|_2$. This uses no inverse of $\Sigma_{1:a}$ and includes $\operatorname{rank}(A)<a$. For every draw $E\le\|A\|_2$; by [F1] it is measurable, so exceptional rank-loss sets do not change its expectation. [given, F1, F2, F3, F5, A1, choose, algebra]

2.1 Put $\sigma=\sigma_{k+1}$ and $R=\sum_{j>k}\sigma_j^2$. If $\sigma=0$, then $R=0$ and all tail singular values vanish, so step 1.1 with $a=k$ gives $E=0$ almost surely. Otherwise $R\ge\sigma^2>0$; set $x=R/(p\sigma^2)>0$ and $b=\sigma\sqrt{\ell/p}$. By [F6], it suffices to prove $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le(1+e\sqrt x)^2$. [step 1.1, F6, algebra]

3.1 Suppose $x\ge1$. Apply the second bound in [F4] to step 1.1 at $a=k$, with oversampling $p$. Since $\|\Sigma_{>k}\|_2=\sigma$ and $\|\Sigma_{>k}\|_F^2=R$ by [F5], $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le p/\ell+e^2(x+1/2) \le1+e^2x+e^2/2\le(1+e\sqrt x)^2.$ The last inequality uses $e<3<4$ from [F7] and $\sqrt x\ge1$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, F5, F7, algebra]

3.2 Suppose $1/7\le x\le1$. The first bound in [F4] at $a=k$ gives $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le1+C(x+1/4)$. Set $y=\sqrt x$ and $a_0=2\sqrt2-e$. The difference $[(1+e\sqrt x)^2-(1+C(x+1/4))]/e$ is $f(y)=2y-a_0y^2-1/\sqrt2$. The series in [F7] gives $27/10<e<11/4$: the partial sum through $1/5!$ is $163/60>27/10$, and the tail after $1/4!$ is at most $(1/5!)\sum_{j\ge0}(1/6)^j=1/100$, so $e\le65/24+1/100=1631/600<11/4$. For the tail estimate, every ratio between successive terms after $1/5!$ is at most $1/6$ by the factorial recurrence, and [F7] sums the resulting geometric majorant. The square comparisons $49/25<2<289/144$ and $7<64/9$ give $7/5<\sqrt2<17/12$ and $\sqrt7<8/3$. Hence $0<a_0<2/15$, $1/\sqrt2<5/7$, and $2/\sqrt7>3/4$. The identity $f((1-t)u+tv)-(1-t)f(u)-tf(v)=a_0t(1-t)(u-v)^2\ge0$ shows $f$ is concave on $[1/\sqrt7,1]$. Therefore it lies above the chord joining its endpoint values, and $f(1/\sqrt7)>3/4-2/105-5/7=1/60>0$, $f(1)>2-2/15-5/7=121/105>0$. This proves $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le(1+e\sqrt x)^2$ throughout the region. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, F7, algebra]

3.3 Suppose $0<x\le1/7$. Let $s=\lfloor p/4\rfloor$, $p'=p-s$, and $a=k+s$. Then $p'\ge\lceil3p/4\rceil\ge2$, $s+1>p/4$, and $a+p'=\ell$, so $1\le a<\ell$. Put $\sigma'=\sigma_{k+s+1}$ and $R'=\sum_{j>k+s}\sigma_j^2$. The first $s+1$ terms in $R$ are at least $(\sigma')^2$, hence $(\sigma')^2\le R/(s+1)$; also $R'\le R$. Apply step 1.1 at this $a$ and the first bound in [F4] with oversampling $p'$. The same sketch and projector are used; only the deterministic SVD partition rank changes. This gives $\mathbb E E^2\le(\sigma')^2+ C\ell(p')^{-2}\bigl(R'+(p'/4)(\sigma')^2\bigr).$ Since $b^2=\sigma^2\ell/p$, $\ell\ge p$, and $p'\ge3p/4$, division yields $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le x\left[\frac{p^2}{\ell(s+1)}+\frac{Cp^2}{(p')^2} +\frac{Cp^2}{4p'(s+1)}\right] \le x\left[4+\frac{16}{9}C+\frac43C\right]=xK^2,$ where $K^2=4+(28/9)C$. These estimates include $p=2,3$, when $s=0$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F4, algebra]

4.1 Since $2<9801/4900$, squaring gives $\sqrt2<99/70$. From this and the bound $e<11/4$ proved in step 3.2, $C<1089/140$ and therefore $K^2<4+(28/9)(1089/140)=141/5$. Since $441/64<7$ and $e>27/10$, we have $\sqrt7+e>213/40$ and $(213/40)^2=45369/1600>141/5$. Thus $K<\sqrt7+e$, and $x\le1/7$ implies $K\sqrt x\le(\sqrt7+e)\sqrt x\le1+e\sqrt x$. Step 3.3 now yields $\mathbb E E^2/b^2\le(1+e\sqrt x)^2$ in the last region. [step 3.2, step 3.3, F7, algebra]

5.1 The cases $x\ge1$, $1/7\le x\le1$, and $0<x\le1/7$ exhaust $x>0$; the zero-tail case was handled in step 2.1. Taking square roots in steps 3.1, 3.2 and 4.1 gives $\mathbb E E\le b(1+e\sqrt x) =\sqrt{\ell/p}\,\sigma+(e\sqrt\ell/p)\sqrt R$. Finally $\sqrt{\ell/p}=\sqrt{1+k/p}\le1+\sqrt{k/p} \le1+\sqrt{k/(p-1)}$, so the original expected-error bound follows without changing its field, dimensions, constants, or sketch width. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Example

Fix the unit cell, a neutral dipole with nonzero total absolute charge $Q$, and
real and reciprocal cutoffs $R,K_c\ge1$. The real-space potential-tail bound
decreases strictly with $\alpha$, while the reciprocal-space potential-tail
bound increases strictly with $\alpha$. Thus choosing $\alpha$ at fixed
cutoffs and target tolerance balances two opposing certified contributions.

1.1 For $\alpha>0$ set $\mathcal R(\alpha)=\frac{QC_R}{\sqrt\pi\alpha}\sum_{m=M_R}^\infty(m+1)^3e^{-\alpha^2m^2}$ and $\mathcal K(\alpha)=\frac{4\pi QC_K}{V}\sum_{m=M_K}^\infty(m+1)^3e^{-m^2/(4\alpha^2)}$, where $M_R=\lfloor R\rfloor$ and $M_K=\lfloor K_c\rfloor$. These are exactly the two bounds in [F1], and they are finite by [F2]. [given, A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 If $0<\alpha_1<\alpha_2$, then for every $m\ge M_R\ge1$, $e^{-\alpha_2^2m^2}/\alpha_2<e^{-\alpha_1^2m^2}/\alpha_1$ because both positive factors strictly decrease. The positive convergent sum therefore gives $\mathcal R(\alpha_2)<\mathcal R(\alpha_1)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 For every $m\ge M_K\ge1$, $e^{-m^2/(4\alpha_2^2)}>e^{-m^2/(4\alpha_1^2)}$, since $\alpha_2>\alpha_1$ makes the negative exponent less negative. Summing positive terms gives $\mathcal K(\alpha_2)>\mathcal K(\alpha_1)$. Hence a fixed-tolerance certificate must balance the real and reciprocal tails; the theorem does not infer an optimal parameter from FFT work or RMS data. [F1, F2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For any finite matrix partition into disjoint blocks, if each local residual satisfies $\|E_b\|_F\le\delta_b$, then the assembled residual satisfies $\|E\|_F\le(\sum_b\delta_b^2)^{1/2}$. In particular, let $A,B$ be conformable finite real or complex matrices, and let $\widetilde A,\widetilde B$ be approximations with $\|A-\widetilde A\|_F\le\epsilon_A$ and $\|B-\widetilde B\|_F\le\epsilon_B$. If a successful block addition or block product from [[alg-hlr-block-addition]] or [[alg-hlr-block-product]] returns $\widehat S$ or $\widehat C$, with disjoint output blocks $b$ and local Frobenius errors $e_b\le\delta_b$, put $\delta=(\sum_b\delta_b^2)^{1/2}$. Then

$$\|A+B-\widehat S\|_F\le\epsilon_A+\epsilon_B+\delta,$$

and

$$\|AB-\widehat C\|_F\le\epsilon_A\|B\|_F+\|A\|_F\epsilon_B+\epsilon_A\epsilon_B+\delta.$$

1.1 Let $\Delta_b$ be the actual residual in output block $b$. For near blocks it is zero; for far blocks [F1] and [F2] give $\|\Delta_b\|_F\le e_b\le\delta_b$. By [F3] their entry supports are disjoint, so [F4] gives $\|\Delta\|_F^2=\sum_b\|\Delta_b\|_F^2\le\sum_b\delta_b^2$. Hence $\|\Delta\|_F\le\delta$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 For addition, write $\widehat S=\widetilde A+\widetilde B+\Delta$. Expanding the squared Frobenius norm as the finite entry inner product and applying [F5] gives the triangle inequality. Therefore $\|A+B-\widehat S\|_F\le\|A-\widetilde A\|_F+\|B-\widetilde B\|_F+\|\Delta\|_F\le\epsilon_A+\epsilon_B+\delta$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For multiplication, put $E_A=\widetilde A-A$ and $E_B=\widetilde B-B$. Since $\widehat C=\widetilde A\widetilde B+\Delta$, expansion gives $AB-\widehat C=-(E_AB+AE_B+E_AE_B+\Delta)$. For any conformable $X,Y$, entrywise Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|(XY)_{ij}|^2\le(\sum_\ell|X_{i\ell}|^2)(\sum_\ell|Y_{\ell j}|^2)$; summing over $i,j$ gives $\|XY\|_F^2\le\|X\|_F^2\|Y\|_F^2$. Thus $\|E_AB\|_F\le\epsilon_A\|B\|_F$, $\|AE_B\|_F\le\|A\|_F\epsilon_B$, and $\|E_AE_B\|_F\le\epsilon_A\epsilon_B$. The triangle inequality from [F4,F5] and step 1.1 give the stated product bound. [F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

source_excerpts: 1.1 Let $h=\lceil\log_2(n/k)\rceil$. By [F1], each split descends one level in either the row tree or the column tree, whose depths are each at most $h$ by [F2]. Hence the block tree has depth at most $2h$. At each level, the first counting hypothesis bounds the total participating far-block side sizes by $2sn$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Each far H block stores at most $k(|\tau|+|\sigma|)$ scalar factor entries. Summing over at most $2h+1$ levels gives $O(sk n(h+1))$ far storage. Every near block has both cluster sizes at most $k$ by [F1], so it stores at most $k^2$ entries; the second counting hypothesis bounds total near storage by $s\lceil n/k\rceil k^2=O(sk n)$ because $k\le n$. This proves the H storage bound. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 In [F5], a far-block product first multiplies an $r_b\times|\sigma|$ factor by $x|_\sigma$ and then a $|\tau|\times r_b$ factor by the result, so it costs $O(k(|\tau|+|\sigma|))$. A near-block product costs $O(|\tau||\sigma|)\le O(k^2)$. The same level and near-block counts used in step 2.1 therefore give H matvec work $O(sk n(h+1))=O(sk n\log_2(2n/k))$. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 By the storage convention in [F4], the leaf row and column bases require at most $2kn$ entries because the leaves partition $I$ and each basis rank is at most $k$. By [F2], each tree has $O(n/k)$ nodes, so all $k\times k$ transfer matrices require $O(kn)$ entries. The third counting hypothesis gives $O(kn)$ entries for all coupling matrices, and step 2.1 bounds dense near blocks by $O(sk n)$. Thus H² storage is $O(sk n)$. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The leaf basis products in [F5] cost $O(kn)$ because their index sets partition $I$ and $J$. Each transfer product costs at most $O(k^2)$ and there are $O(n/k)$ internal clusters by [F2]; each coupling product costs at most $O(k^2)$ and the third hypothesis bounds their number by $s\lceil n/k\rceil$. Dense near products cost $O(sk n)$ by step 2.1. Summing gives H² matvec work $O(sk n)$. [F2, F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron
with connected boundary, and let $X$ be the full-kernel orthogonal gauge of
[[def-na-pe11-maxwell-cavity-eigenproblem]]. Every sequence in $X$ bounded in
$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging strongly in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$. Equivalently, the inclusion of $X$, with its
$H(\operatorname{curl})$ graph norm, into $L^2$ is compact. Moreover there
is a constant $C_\Omega$ such that
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \qquad(u\in X).$$
Thus the curl form is coercive on $X$ in its $H(\operatorname{curl})$ graph
norm.

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded contractible Lipschitz polyhedron
with connected boundary, and let $X$ be the full-kernel orthogonal gauge of
[[def-na-pe11-maxwell-cavity-eigenproblem]]. Every sequence in $X$ bounded in
$H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging strongly in
$L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$. Equivalently, the inclusion of $X$, with its
$H(\operatorname{curl})$ graph norm, into $L^2$ is compact. Moreover there
is a constant $C_\Omega$ such that
$$\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \qquad(u\in X).$$
Thus the curl form is coercive on $X$ in its $H(\operatorname{curl})$ graph
norm.

1.1 By [F1] and Countable Choice [A2], choose for each $n$ $z_n\in H_0^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ and $p_n\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $u_n=z_n+\nabla p_n$ and $\|z_n\|_{H^1}\le C_\Omega\|u_n\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}$. Hence $(z_n)$ is bounded in $W_0^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$. [A2, F1, given, choose]

1.2 Set $g_n:=\nabla p_n=u_n-z_n$. By [F3], $z_n\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$; since $u_n\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$, their difference is in that space. Its distributional curl is zero: for every compactly supported smooth vector test $\varphi$, integration by parts in the weak-derivative definition gives $\langle\operatorname{curl}\nabla p_n,\varphi\rangle =-\int_\Omega p_n\,\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}\varphi)\,dx=0$, because $\operatorname{div}(\operatorname{curl}\varphi)=0$. Thus $g_n\in K$ for the kernel $K$ defining $X$. [F3, given, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] componentwise and take the finite successive subsequence to obtain indices $n_j$ for which $z_{n_j}$ converges strongly, and therefore is Cauchy, in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$. The finite product of the three component $L^2$ norms is the vector $L^2$ norm. [A1, A2, F2, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 For any $j,k$, $u_{n_j}-u_{n_k}\in X=K^\perp$ and $g_{n_j}-g_{n_k}\in K$, so their $L^2$ inner product is zero. Since $u_{n_j}-u_{n_k}=(z_{n_j}-z_{n_k})+(g_{n_j}-g_{n_k})$, it follows that $\|u_{n_j}-u_{n_k}\|_2^2=\langle u_{n_j}-u_{n_k},z_{n_j}-z_{n_k}\rangle_{L^2}$. Cauchy–Schwarz implies $\|u_{n_j}-u_{n_k}\|_2\le\|z_{n_j}-z_{n_k}\|_2$ (with the zero case immediate). Step 2.1 therefore makes $(u_{n_j})$ Cauchy in $L^2$; [F4] gives its strong $L^2$ limit. This proves compactness. [F1, F4, F6, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra]

4.1 If the curl Poincare inequality failed, Countable Choice [A2] selects for each $n$ $v_n\in X$ with $\|v_n\|_2=1$ and $\|\operatorname{curl}v_n\|_2<1/n$. The graph norms are bounded, so compactness proved in steps 1.1–3.1 gives a subsequence converging strongly in $L^2$ to some $v$. By [F5], after a further subsequence $v\in H_0(\operatorname{curl})$ and $\operatorname{curl}v=0$. For each $k\in K$, strong convergence and $v_n\perp K$ give $(v,k)_{L^2}=0$, so $v\in X\cap K=\{0\}$. But strong convergence preserves $\|v\|_2=1$, a contradiction. Therefore a uniform constant $C_\Omega$ exists. [A2, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 3.1, given, choose]

5.1 The estimate in step 4.1 makes $\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl})}^2=\|u\|_2^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2^2$ bounded by a constant times $\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_2^2$ on $X$. Hence the curl form is coercive in the graph norm. [step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the data of [[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]] and
assume the local spaces span $V$. Suppose $0<C_0,C_1<\infty$ satisfy:

- for every $x\in V$, there are local vectors $z_i$ such that
  $x=\sum_iR_i z_i$ and $\sum_i z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i\le C_0\|x\|_A^2$;
- for every tuple $(z_i)$,
  $\|\sum_iR_i z_i\|_A^2\le C_1\sum_i z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i$.

For an $A$-self-adjoint positive operator $T$, define
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(T)=\inf_{x\ne0}\frac{a(Tx,x)}{a(x,x)},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(T)=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{a(Tx,x)}{a(x,x)},\qquad \kappa_A(T)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}^A(T)}{\lambda_{\min}^A(T)}. $$
Then the exact additive Schwarz operator $T=BA$ is $A$-self-adjoint positive and
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(BA)\ge C_0^{-1},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(BA)\le C_1,\qquad \kappa_A(BA)\le C_0C_1. $$
If the inexact local matrices satisfy
$\alpha A_i\preceq\widetilde A_i\preceq\beta A_i$ for
$0<\alpha\le\beta$, then
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(\widetilde BA)\ge(\beta C_0)^{-1},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(\widetilde BA)\le C_1/\alpha,\qquad \kappa_A(\widetilde BA)\le(\beta/\alpha)C_0C_1. $$

1.1 The stable-decomposition hypothesis implies that the local spaces span $V$, so [F3] makes $B$ SPD. Each $\Pi_i$ is $A$-self-adjoint by [F2], hence $T=BA=\sum_i\Pi_i$ is $A$-self-adjoint. Moreover $a(Tx,x)=\sum_i\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2\ge0$; if this is zero, then every $\Pi_i x=0$. For any $v_i\in V_i$, [F2] gives $\Pi_i v_i=v_i$, so $a(x,v_i)=a(\Pi_i x,v_i)=0$. The spaces span $V$, hence $x=0$ and $T$ is positive. [F1, F2, F3, given]

1.2 Fix $x\ne0$ and choose the decomposition $x=\sum_iR_i z_i$ from the stable-decomposition hypothesis. Orthogonal projection gives $\|x\|_A^2 =\sum_i a(x,R_i z_i) =\sum_i a(\Pi_i x,R_i z_i) \le \left(\sum_i\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\sum_i z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i\right)^{1/2}.$ The last inequality is [F5] in the product inner product on the finite tuple space. 1.3 For each $x$, write $\Pi_i x=R_i y_i$ with $y_i=A_i^{-1}R_i^{\mathsf T}Ax$. The synthesis hypothesis and [F2] give $\|Tx\|_A^2 =\left\|\sum_iR_i y_i\right\|_A^2 \le C_1\sum_i\|\Pi_i x\|_A^2 =C_1a(Tx,x).$ Set $q=a(Tx,x)/\|x\|_A^2$. ## Statement

Use the data of [[def-overlapping-schwarz-subspace-correction-data]] and
assume the local spaces span $V$. Suppose $0<C_0,C_1<\infty$ satisfy:

- for every $x\in V$, there are local vectors $z_i$ such that
  $x=\sum_iR_i z_i$ and $\sum_i z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i\le C_0\|x\|_A^2$;
- for every tuple $(z_i)$,
  $\|\sum_iR_i z_i\|_A^2\le C_1\sum_i z_i^{\mathsf T}A_i z_i$.

For an $A$-self-adjoint positive operator $T$, define
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(T)=\inf_{x\ne0}\frac{a(Tx,x)}{a(x,x)},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(T)=\sup_{x\ne0}\frac{a(Tx,x)}{a(x,x)},\qquad \kappa_A(T)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}^A(T)}{\lambda_{\min}^A(T)}. $$
Then the exact additive Schwarz operator $T=BA$ is $A$-self-adjoint positive and
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(BA)\ge C_0^{-1},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(BA)\le C_1,\qquad \kappa_A(BA)\le C_0C_1. $$
If the inexact local matrices satisfy
$\alpha A_i\preceq\widetilde A_i\preceq\beta A_i$ for
$0<\alpha\le\beta$, then
$$ \lambda_{\min}^A(\widetilde BA)\ge(\beta C_0)^{-1},\qquad \lambda_{\max}^A(\widetilde BA)\le C_1/\alpha,\qquad \kappa_A(\widetilde BA)\le(\beta/\alpha)C_0C_1. $$

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $k>0$ and real $\eta\ne0$, and use the smooth-boundary geometry, spaces and operator $A_{k,\eta}$ of [[def-bem-smooth-helmholtz-combined-field-operator]]. Then $A_{k,\eta}$ extends to a bounded bijection on complex $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ with bounded inverse. In particular, for this fixed $k,\eta$ there is a finite constant $C_{k,\eta}=\|A_{k,\eta}^{-1}\|$ such that
$$\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}\le C_{k,\eta}\|A_{k,\eta}\phi\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}.$$
The constant can also depend on $\Gamma$; no bound uniform as $k$ varies is asserted. For every boundary datum $f\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, $u=D_kA_{k,\eta}^{-1}f-i\eta S_kA_{k,\eta}^{-1}f$ is the unique outgoing weak exterior Dirichlet solution with trace $f$ in the local $H^1$ class of [[thm-bem-exterior-helmholtz-dirichlet-uniqueness]].

1.1 Suppose $A_{k,\eta}\phi=0$ and set $u=D_k\phi-i\eta S_k\phi$. Here $\phi\in H^{1/2}$ is a valid single-layer density by the continuous inclusions $H^{1/2}\subset L^2\subset H^{-1/2}$, the last inclusion following from Cauchy–Schwarz and the continuous $H^{1/2}\to L^2$ embedding. By [F2], $u^+$ is outgoing, weak Helmholtz and has zero exterior trace. [F3] gives $u^+=0$, so also $\partial_n^+u=0$. [F2, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 By [F2], $\gamma^-u-\gamma^+u=-\phi$, so $\gamma^-u=-\phi$. The conormal jump is $\partial_n^-u-\partial_n^+u=-i\eta\phi$, whence $\partial_n^-u=-i\eta\phi=i\eta\gamma^-u$. The products here use the $L^2$ realization of $H^{1/2}$ as an element of its dual $H^{-1/2}$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The interior weak Green identity [F2] tested with $u^-$ gives $\int_{\Omega^-}(|\nabla u^-|^2-k^2|u^-|^2)dx=\langle\partial_n^-u,\gamma^-u\rangle=i\eta\|\gamma^-u\|_{L^2(\Gamma)}^2.$ The left side is real. Taking imaginary parts and using real $\eta\ne0$ gives $\gamma^-u=0$, and step 2.1 gives $\phi=0$. Thus $A_{k,\eta}$ is injective. [F2, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 By [F1], $2A_{k,\eta}=I-\mathcal K_{k,\eta}$ with compact $\mathcal K_{k,\eta}$. Injectivity and [F4] make $I-\mathcal K_{k,\eta}$ boundedly invertible, hence so is $A_{k,\eta}$. Its finite inverse norm gives the estimate. For a prescribed $f$, use $\phi=A_{k,\eta}^{-1}f$; [F2] gives the outgoing solution and the operator identity gives its trace $f$. The difference of any two such solutions satisfies [F3], proving uniqueness. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, given, construct, algebra] ∎

Then $a(e_1+\nabla\chi_1)=ce_1$, whose divergence is zero, so it satisfies the cell equation. Uniqueness [F2] identifies it as the first corrector; its mean flux is $ce_1$. [F2, F1, algebra]

Its mean flux is $\int_Ya(y_1)e_j=(\rho a_1+(1-\rho)a_2)e_j$. These columns yield the displayed diagonal matrix. [F3, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Let $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,1)$, and $C=(2,2+\delta)$ with
$\delta=2^{-51}$, using binary64 inputs. The exact orientation determinant is
$\delta>0$. In the 53-bit filter system with $u=2^{-53}$, the outward error
interval includes zero, so the certified predicate uses its exact integer
fallback and returns positive.

1.1 With rows $(A,1),(B,1),(C,1)$, the determinant is $\det\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\1&1&1\\2&2+\delta&1\end{pmatrix}=\delta$ by expansion along the first row. Thus the exact sign is positive. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 In lexicographic Leibniz order the only nonzero signed terms are $+(2+\delta)$ and $-2$. They and their sum $\delta$ are exactly representable normal binary64 values, so by [A1] the filter's approximation is $\widehat D=\delta$. [given, F2, A1, algebra]

1.3 The absolute-term sum is $S=(2+\delta)+2=4+2^{-51}$. Since $4\le S<8$, [F4] gives spacing $2^{-50}$; $S$ is halfway between $4$ and $4+2^{-50}$. Outward upward rounding therefore gives $U=4+2^{-50}$ by [F5], and the outward DAG is sound by [F6]. [F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 Here $s=3$, so $q=7$ and $\gamma_7>7u$. Therefore $E\ge\gamma_7U>28\cdot2^{-53}=7\delta>\delta=\widehat D$. The filter interval contains zero and [F7] forces `inconclusive`. [F2, F3, F7, step 1.3, algebra]

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice, let $\alpha<2$, $\rho=1-\alpha$, $n\ge1$, and let $G\in C^{2n}$ in each coordinate on $[0,1]^2$. Let $\widetilde p_{n,\rho}$ and $\widetilde p_{n,0}$ be the monic node polynomials of the pushed-forward Gauss–Jacobi rules for $r^\rho dr$ and $ds$, respectively. Define
$$M_\rho=\int_0^1r^\rho dr=\frac1{\rho+1},\quad K_\rho=\frac1{(2n)!_{\mathbb R}}\int_0^1\widetilde p_{n,\rho}(r)^2r^\rho dr,\quad K_0=\frac1{(2n)!_{\mathbb R}}\int_0^1\widetilde p_{n,0}(s)^2ds.$$
Then the rule of [[alg-duffy-weighted-product-gauss-quadrature]] satisfies
$$\left|\int_T\|(x,y)\|_2^{-\alpha}q(x,y)\,dx\,dy-Q_{n,\alpha}^{D}(G)\right| \le K_\rho\|\partial_r^{2n}G\|_\infty+M_\rho K_0\|\partial_s^{2n}G\|_\infty,$$
where $G$ is the transformed amplitude from [[thm-duffy-weak-singularity-transform]].

1.1 The exponent $\rho=1-\alpha$ satisfies $\rho>-1$. By [F5] and [A1], the Jacobi weights $(1+t)^\rho$ and $1$ define finite positive measures with full support; the affine node/weight scalings in [F2] give their Gaussian rules for $r^\rho dr$ and $ds$. [A1, F2, F5, given, algebra]

1.2 The first measure has mass $M_\rho=1/(\rho+1)$ by [F6], and the second has mass $1$. For the first affine pushforward, $r=(1+t)/2$ gives $r^\rho dr=2^{-(\rho+1)}(1+t)^\rho dt$ and its monic node polynomial is $\widetilde p_{n,\rho}(r)=2^{-n}p_{n,\rho}(2r-1)$. Hence its squared-node-polynomial integral is $2^{-(\rho+1+2n)}\int_{-1}^1p_{n,\rho}(t)^2(1+t)^\rho dt$. The derivative of $H((1+t)/2)$ contributes $2^{-2n}$, so [F3] gives exactly $K_\rho$ as defined. The same calculation with $\rho=0$ gives $K_0$. Positivity of the factorial denominator follows from [F7]. [F2, F3, F6, F7, algebra]
2.1 Apply [F4] to the transformed integral and tensor rule identified by [F1]–[F2]. Substituting the masses and constants from step 1.2 yields the displayed error bound. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2] ∎
