## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses in [[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]] on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain in dimension two or three. For every $F\in V'$ and $f\in Q$, there is a unique $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ solving
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v),\qquad b(u,q)=-\int_Dfq$$
for all $v\in V,q\in Q$. The graph norm on the flux and zero-mean pressure norm make these equations well-posed; the mean-zero pressure convention fixes the Neumann gauge.

1.1 The form bounds follow from the permeability eigenvalue bounds: $|a(u,v)|\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}\|u\|_{L^2}\|v\|_{L^2}\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}\|u\|_V\|v\|_V$, and $|b(v,q)|\le\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2\|q\|_2\le\|v\|_V\|q\|_Q$. Thus $M_a\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}$ and $M_b\le1$. [given, F1, algebra]
1.2 For $q\in Q$, the right inverse [F3] gives $B_Dq\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, so [F7] places $B_Dq$ in $V$. Its graph norm is finite. [A1, F3, F7, construct]

1.3 Define $B:V\to Q$ by $(Bv,q)_Q=b(v,q)$. Since $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\operatorname{div}v$ and [F2] places the divergence in $Q$, $Bv=-\operatorname{div}v$. Hence $Z=\ker B=\{v\in V:\operatorname{div}v=0\}$; it is closed because divergence is continuous in the graph norm. For $v\in Z$, the graph norm equals $\|v\|_2$, and $a(v,v)\ge\kappa_{\max}^{-1}\|v\|_2^2=\kappa_{\max}^{-1}\|v\|_V^2$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For nonzero $q\in Q$, choose $v=-B_Dq$. Then $b(v,q)=\|q\|_2^2$ by [F3]. The Poincare bound [F4] gives $\|B_Dq\|_V^2=\|B_Dq\|_2^2+\|q\|_2^2\le(1+L^2C_{\rm div}^2)\|q\|_2^2$. Therefore the inf-sup constant for $b$ on $V\times Q$ is at least $(1+L^2C_{\rm div}^2)^{-1/2}>0$. [F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 If $Q=\{0\}$, [F2] makes $Z=V$, so the Countable Choice Lax–Milgram branch of [F5] applies using coercivity from step 1.3. If $Q\ne\{0\}$, [F3] supplies a nonzero $q$; then $B_Dq\in V$ by step 1.2 and is nonzero since its divergence is $q$. The positive inf-sup from step 2.1 and the nonzero Hilbert spaces [F1] allow the mixed branch of [F5]. In both cases boundedness from step 1.1, closedness and coercivity from step 1.3, and data functionals $F$ and $G(q)=-\int_Dfq$ satisfy [F5]; [F6] makes $G$ bounded. The theorem gives the asserted unique pair, and the pressure mean-zero condition removes the additive constant. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra, cases] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and the hypotheses in [[def-na-neumann-darcy-mixed-problem]] on a bounded connected Lipschitz domain in dimension two or three. For every $F\in V'$ and $f\in Q$, there is a unique $(u,p)\in V\times Q$ solving
$$a(u,v)+b(v,p)=F(v),\qquad b(u,q)=-\int_Dfq$$
for all $v\in V,q\in Q$. The graph norm on the flux and zero-mean pressure norm make these equations well-posed; the mean-zero pressure convention fixes the Neumann gauge.

1.1 The form bounds follow from the permeability eigenvalue bounds: $|a(u,v)|\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}\|u\|_{L^2}\|v\|_{L^2}\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}\|u\|_V\|v\|_V$, and $|b(v,q)|\le\|\operatorname{div}v\|_2\|q\|_2\le\|v\|_V\|q\|_Q$. Thus $M_a\le\kappa_{\min}^{-1}$ and $M_b\le1$. [given, F1, algebra]
1.2 For $q\in Q$, the right inverse [F3] gives $B_Dq\in H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, so [F7] places $B_Dq$ in $V$. Its graph norm is finite. [A1, F3, F7, construct]

1.3 Define $B:V\to Q$ by $(Bv,q)_Q=b(v,q)$. Since $b(v,q)=-\int_Dq\operatorname{div}v$ and [F2] places the divergence in $Q$, $Bv=-\operatorname{div}v$. Hence $Z=\ker B=\{v\in V:\operatorname{div}v=0\}$; it is closed because divergence is continuous in the graph norm. For $v\in Z$, the graph norm equals $\|v\|_2$, and $a(v,v)\ge\kappa_{\max}^{-1}\|v\|_2^2=\kappa_{\max}^{-1}\|v\|_V^2$. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 For nonzero $q\in Q$, choose $v=-B_Dq$. Then $b(v,q)=\|q\|_2^2$ by [F3]. The Poincare bound [F4] gives $\|B_Dq\|_V^2=\|B_Dq\|_2^2+\|q\|_2^2\le(1+L^2C_{\rm div}^2)\|q\|_2^2$. Therefore the inf-sup constant for $b$ on $V\times Q$ is at least $(1+L^2C_{\rm div}^2)^{-1/2}>0$. [F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 If $Q=\{0\}$, [F2] makes $Z=V$, so the Countable Choice Lax–Milgram branch of [F5] applies using coercivity from step 1.3. If $Q\ne\{0\}$, [F3] supplies a nonzero $q$; then $B_Dq\in V$ by step 1.2 and is nonzero since its divergence is $q$. The positive inf-sup from step 2.1 and the nonzero Hilbert spaces [F1] allow the mixed branch of [F5]. In both cases boundedness from step 1.1, closedness and coercivity from step 1.3, and data functionals $F$ and $G(q)=-\int_Dfq$ satisfy [F5]; [F6] makes $G$ bounded. The theorem gives the asserted unique pair, and the pressure mean-zero condition removes the additive constant. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra, cases] ∎

## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $W:H^{1/2}(\Gamma)\to H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ be the hypersingular operator of [[def-bem-calderon-boundary-operators]]. It is symmetric and nonnegative, its kernel is exactly the constants, and there is $c>0$ such that
$$\langle W\phi,\phi\rangle_\Gamma\ge c\inf_{a\in\mathbb R}\|\phi-a\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)}^2.$$
The real scalar $m_\Gamma(\phi):=\int_\Gamma\phi\,dS$ is the $L^2$ integral, not a pairing of two elements of $H^{1/2}$. The continuous embeddings $H^{1/2}\subset L^2\subset H^{-1/2}$ use the fixed Hilbert chart convention; the second map sends $f$ to the functional $g\mapsto\int_\Gamma fg\,dS$. Thus $m_\Gamma(\phi)$ can equivalently be evaluated by pairing this realized negative-order functional with $1$. The stabilized form
$$b(\phi,\psi)=\langle W\phi,\psi\rangle_\Gamma+m_\Gamma(\phi)m_\Gamma(\psi)$$
is bounded and coercive on $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. Consequently, for each $f\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$ there is a unique $\phi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ such that $b(\phi,\psi)=\langle f,\psi\rangle_\Gamma$ for every $\psi\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$.

2.1 Let $u=D\phi$ and set $a=u^-_{\Omega^-}$. By [F3], $\|\gamma^-u^- -a\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|\nabla u^-\|_2$. By [F4], $\|\gamma^+u^+\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|\nabla u^+\|_2$. The jump condition gives $\phi+a=-(\gamma^-u^- -a)+\gamma^+u^+$, so $\inf_{c\in\mathbb R}\|\phi-c\|_{H^{1/2}}\le\|\phi+a\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\mathcal E(D\phi)^{1/2}.$ Together with step 1.1 this proves the quotient ellipticity inequality. If $\phi$ is constant, the pair $(-\phi,0)$ belongs to $\mathcal A_\phi$ and has zero energy, so it is the unique minimizer and step 1.1 gives $W\phi=0$. Conversely, if $W\phi=0$, the ellipticity inequality makes $\phi$ a limit in $H^{1/2}$ of constants; the constant subspace is closed because it is finite dimensional, so $\phi$ is constant. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Put $\bar\phi=|\Gamma|^{-1}m_\Gamma(\phi)$ and $\phi_0=\phi-\bar\phi$. The quotient norm controls $\|\phi_0\|_{H^{1/2}}$: for any constant $a$, the $L^2$ bound gives $|\bar\phi-a|\le |\Gamma|^{-1/2}\|\phi-a\|_{L^2}$, hence $\|\phi_0\|_{H^{1/2}}\le C\|\phi-a\|_{H^{1/2}}$, and take the infimum. Also $|\bar\phi|=|m_\Gamma(\phi)|/|\Gamma|$. Thus $\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}}^2\le C(\inf_a\|\phi-a\|_{H^{1/2}}^2+|m_\Gamma(\phi)|^2)$. By [F2], $W$ is bounded; the rank-one term is bounded because $|m_\Gamma(\phi)|\le|\Gamma|^{1/2}\|\phi\|_{L^2}\le C\|\phi\|_{H^{1/2}}$, so $b$ is bounded. Its coercivity follows from step 2.1 and the last decomposition. [F2, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 The space $H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$ is a real Hilbert space under the square-sum chart norm fixed in [[def-bem-lipschitz-polyhedral-boundary-and-trace-spaces]]. Apply [F5] to the bounded coercive form $b$ and the bounded functional $\psi\mapsto\langle f,\psi\rangle$; it yields a unique solution for every $f\in H^{-1/2}(\Gamma)$. [F5, step 3.1, given, construct] ∎

## Statement

Let $A=[-1,1]$, $b(a)=a$, and $\ell(a)=a^2$. Then
$$H(p)=\max_{a\in[-1,1]}(-ap-a^2)= \begin{cases} p^2/4,&|p|\le2,\\ |p|-1,&|p|>2. \end{cases}$$
For $m\ge1$, let $A_m=\{-1+2r/m:r=0,\ldots,m\}$ and let
$H_m(p)=\max_{a\in A_m}(-ap-a^2)$. The uniform control-grid error satisfies
$$\sup_{p\in\mathbb R}|H_m(p)-H(p)|\le m^{-2}.$$
Thus $A_m$ satisfies the control approximation hypothesis of
[[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]]. For any continuous periodic initial
datum, its semi-Lagrangian scheme falls under
[[thm-na-first-order-hjb-scheme-convergence]] whenever the stated mesh
restrictions also hold.

## Statement

Let $A=[-1,1]$, $b(a)=a$, and $\ell(a)=a^2$. Then

For $m\ge1$, let $A_m=\{-1+2r/m:r=0,\ldots,m\}$ and let

Thus $A_m$ satisfies the control approximation hypothesis of
[[def-na-first-order-hjb-cauchy-problem]]. For any continuous periodic initial
datum, its semi-Lagrangian scheme falls under
[[thm-na-first-order-hjb-scheme-convergence]] whenever the stated mesh
restrictions also hold.

1.1 Completing the square as in [F1], the unconstrained maximizing control is $a_*=-p/2$. It lies in $[-1,1]$ exactly when $|p|\le2$, where substitution gives $H(p)=p^2/4$. If $p>2$, the concave quadratic is maximized at $a=-1$ and gives $p-1$; if $p<-2$, it is maximized at $a=1$ and gives $-p-1$. This proves the displayed formula. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For $|p|\le2$, choose a nearest $a_m\in A_m$ to $a_*$. Then $$H(p)-H_m(p)=(a_m-a_*)^2\le m^{-2}$$ by [F1] and [F2]. For $|p|>2$, the maximizing endpoint belongs to $A_m$, so $H_m(p)=H(p)$. Also $H_m(p)\le H(p)$ since $A_m\subset A$. Taking the supremum proves the global error bound. Because $m^{-2}\to0$, condition [F3] is satisfied for every bounded momentum set (in fact for all momenta), so the stated convergence theorem applies along any mesh family satisfying its remaining hypotheses. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $n\ge1$, $0\le d<n$, $x_0<\cdots<x_n$, and
$h=\max_j(x_{j+1}-x_j)$. Let $D_d(x)=\sum_{j=0}^n w_j/(x-x_j)$ be the
Floater–Hormann denominator from
[[def-floater-hormann-interpolant]]. For every open gap
$x_\alpha<x<x_{\alpha+1}$,
$$|D_d(x)|\ge \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{d!\,h^{d+1}}, & d\ge1,\\[4pt] \dfrac{1}{h(1+\beta)}, & d=0, \end{cases}$$
where $\beta$ is the local ratio of
[[def-floater-hormann-local-mesh-ratio]].

1.1 Suppose $d\ge1$. The middle block $I_2$ contains at least one index: $j=\max(0,\alpha-d+1)$ satisfies $j\le\alpha$, $j+d\ge\alpha+1$, and $j\le n-d$. Thus its window contains both endpoints of the gap and $\mu_j(x)>0$. By [F2], $s(x)=s_1(x)+s_2(x)+s_3(x)\ge s_2(x)\ge\mu_j(x)$, with empty block sums interpreted as zero. From [F1], $$|D_d(x)|=\frac{s(x)}{\prod_{k=0}^{n}|x-x_k|} \ge\frac{\mu_j(x)}{\prod_{k=0}^{n}|x-x_k|} =|\lambda_j(x)| =\frac{1}{\prod_{k=j}^{j+d}|x-x_k|}.$$ This reduces the denominator estimate to one window product. [given, F1, F2, choose, algebra]

1.2 Now let $d=0$. On the first gap, $I_1=\{0\}$ and the other nonempty block sums are positive by [F2], hence $s\ge\mu_0$ and $|D_0(x)|\ge|\lambda_0(x)|=1/(x-x_0)\ge1/h$. On the last gap it gives $I_3=\{n\}$ and the other nonempty block sums are positive, hence $s\ge\mu_n$ and $|D_0(x)|\ge1/(x_n-x)\ge1/h$. These bounds imply the claimed inequality because $\beta\ge0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Put $u=\alpha-j+1$ and $v=j+d-\alpha$, so $u,v\ge1$ and $u+v=d+1$. For $j\le k\le\alpha$, $|x-x_k|\le x_{\alpha+1}-x_k\le(\alpha+1-k)h$; for $\alpha+1\le k\le j+d$, $|x-x_k|\le x_k-x_\alpha\le(k-\alpha)h$. Multiplying these $d+1$ bounds gives $$\prod_{k=j}^{j+d}|x-x_k|\le u!\,v!\,h^{d+1}\le d!\,h^{d+1}.$$ The last inequality follows from $\binom{d+1}{u}=(d+1)!/(u!v!)\ge d+1$. Substitution in step 1.1 proves the $d\ge1$ bound. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $1\le\alpha\le n-2$, both $I_1$ and $I_3$ are nonempty. The first two terms from $I_3$ and first two read backward from $I_1$ form positive pairs. With $\Delta=x_{\alpha+1}-x_\alpha$, $\delta_R=x_{\alpha+2}-x_{\alpha+1}$ and $\delta_L=x_\alpha-x_{\alpha-1}$, [F1]–[F2] yield $$|D_0(x)|\ge \max\left\{ \frac1{x_{\alpha+1}-x}-\frac1{x_{\alpha+2}-x}, \frac1{x-x_\alpha}-\frac1{x-x_{\alpha-1}} \right\}.$$ Writing $t=x_{\alpha+1}-x\le\Delta$ in the first difference gives $\delta_R/[t(t+\delta_R)]\ge 1/[h(1+\Delta/\delta_R)]$. Writing $u=x-x_\alpha\le\Delta$ in the second gives $\delta_L/[u(u+\delta_L)]\ge 1/[h(1+\Delta/\delta_L)]$. Hence $$|D_0(x)|\ge \frac{1}{h\left(1+\min\{\Delta/\delta_L,\Delta/\delta_R\}\right)} \ge\frac1{h(1+\beta)}$$ by [F3]. For $n\le2$ there is no such interior index, so steps 1.2 cover all gaps. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

whereas the complementary recurrence solution $D_n(1)$ defined in

solution $\widetilde J_n=J_n(1)-\varepsilon D_n(1)$ is negative for some

1.1 Let $a_k=(1/2)^{2k+n}/(k!(k+n)!)$. By [F2], the positive terms $a_k$ decrease strictly to zero. Grouping the alternating series in consecutive pairs gives $J_n(1)=(a_0-a_1)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots>0$. Also $(k+n)!\ge n!$, so $$0<J_n(1)\le\sum_{k\ge0}a_k \le\frac{2^{-n}}{n!}\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(1/4)^k}{k!} =\frac{2^{-n}e^{1/4}}{n!}\longrightarrow0.$$ In particular, $J_0(1)\ge1-1/4=3/4$ and $J_1(1)\ge1/2-1/16=7/16$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By [F4], $D_0(1)=-J_1(1)<0$ and $D_1(1)=J_0(1)>0$; hence $D_2=2D_1-D_0>D_1>0$. If $n\ge2$ and $D_n\ge D_{n-1}>0$, then $D_{n+1}=2nD_n-D_{n-1}\ge(2n-1)D_n\ge3D_n$. Induction gives $D_n\ge3^{n-2}D_2$ for $n\ge2$, so $D_n\to\infty$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, induction]

3.1 The exact sequence $J_n-\varepsilon D_n$ obeys the same linear recurrence by [F3] and [F4], so it is the forward-recurrence solution from the displayed perturbed seeds. Since $J_n\to0$ and $D_n\to\infty$ by steps 1.1 and 2.1, some finite $n$ satisfies $\varepsilon D_n>J_n$. At that index $\widetilde J_n<0<J_n$. ## Example

For $0<T\le\tfrac14$, the upward formula for the first two Boys orders is
$$F_1(T)=\frac{F_0(T)-e^{-T}}{2T}.$$
Both subtracted quantities are close to one, while their difference is of order $T$. If the input intervals for them have radii $r_0,r_e$, the propagated upward interval radius is bounded by $(r_0+r_e)/(2T)$ plus endpoint-rounding error. Thus fixed input radii can be strongly amplified as $T\downarrow0$. The direct Taylor branch has the certified remainder $T^2/10$ for $F_0$ after its linear term, so it avoids this division by a small $T$.

Suppose $(u,p)$ is a strong solution of the no-slip Navier–Stokes equations with forcing $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$ and $u\in W^{1,\infty}(0,T;H^2(D)^d\cap V_\sigma)$ and $p\in W^{1,\infty}(0,T;H^1(D)\cap L^2_0(D))$. Set
$$M:=1+\|u\|_{W^{1,\infty}H^2}+\|p\|_{W^{1,\infty}H^1},\quad M_u:=\|u\|_{L^\infty V},$$
$$M_\infty:=\bigl(\|u_0\|_2^2+C_P(D)^2\nu^{-1}\|f\|_{L^2L^2}^2\bigr)^{1/2},\quad M_E:=\nu^{-1/2}\|u_0\|_2+C_P(D)\nu^{-1}\|f\|_{L^2L^2},$$
and $\Lambda:=1+C_D\nu^{-3}M_u^4$, where $C_D$ depends only on the domain, dimension and the trilinear-form constant. For sufficiently fine time partitions satisfying $\tau_{\max}\Lambda\le\tfrac12$, initialize by $u_h^0=P_{Z_h}u_0$ and choose any backward Euler MINI solution. Then
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|u(t_n)-u_h^n\|_2+\nu^{1/2}\left(\sum_{n=1}^N\tau_n\|u(t_n)-u_h^n\|_V^2\right)^{1/2}\le C_*\bigl(hM+\tau_{\max}M^2\bigr),$$
where one may take
$$C_*:=C_{D,\mathrm{shape}}(1+\nu)^2(1+\nu^{-4})(1+T)^2(1+M_\infty+M_E+M)^4\exp(2T\Lambda).$$
Here $f$ is the forcing of the strong solution and $C_{D,\mathrm{shape}}$ is independent of $h$, all time steps, and $\nu$. ## Statement

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $D\subset\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, bounded, connected and Lipschitz, with $d\in\{2,3\}$, let $0<T<\infty$ and $\nu>0$. Use $V=H^1_0(D;\mathbb R^d)$, $Q=L^2_0(D)$, $V_\sigma=\ker(\operatorname{div}:V\to Q)$, $H_\sigma=\overline{V_\sigma}^{\,L^2(D)}$, the bilinear form $a_\nu(v,w)=2\nu\int_D\varepsilon(v):\varepsilon(w)$, the pressure form $b(v,q)=-(q,\operatorname{div}v)_{L^2}$, and the real skew convective form $c$ from [[def-na-stokes-zero-mean-pressure-and-velocity-spaces]], [[def-na-evolutionary-skew-convective-form]] and [[def-na-solenoidal-energy-weak-ns-velocity]]. Let $C_P$ be a Poincare constant, $C_{\rm div}$ a bounded divergence-right-inverse constant, and choose $C_c$ large enough that
$$|c(a;b,v)|\le C_c\|a\|_V\|b\|_V\|v\|_V,\qquad \|c(a;a,\cdot)\|_{V^*}\le C_c\|a\|_{L^2}^{1/2}\|a\|_V^{3/2}.$$
For $f\in L^2(0,T;L^2(D)^d)$ and $u_0\in H_\sigma$, let $u$ be a solenoidal energy weak velocity. Put $U=\|u\|_{L^\infty L^2}$, $E=\|u\|_{L^2V}$ and $F=\|f\|_{L^2L^2}$. There is a unique $P\in L^\infty(0,T;Q)\cap C_w([0,T];Q)$ with $P(0)=0$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $v\in V$,
$$ (u(t)-u_0,v)_{L^2}+\int_0^t\bigl(a_\nu(u(s),v)+c(u(s);u(s),v)\bigr)\,ds+b(v,P(t))=\int_0^t(f(s),v)_{L^2}\,ds.$$
Here $C_w$ means continuity when tested against every fixed element of the Hilbert space $Q$. Moreover,
$$\|P\|_{L^\infty Q}\le C_{\rm div}\bigl(C_P(U+\|u_0\|_{L^2})+C_P\sqrt T F+2\nu\sqrt T E+C_cT^{1/4}U^{1/2}E^{3/2}\bigr).$$
Define the $Q$-valued time distribution $p=\partial_tP$ by
$$\langle p,\eta\rangle=-\int_0^TP(t)\eta'(t)\,dt\qquad(\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)).$$
The bound $\|\langle p,\eta\rangle\|_Q\le\|P\|_{L^\infty Q}\|\eta'\|_{L^1}$ makes this a continuous linear map from scalar test functions to $Q$. Then $p$ is the unique mean-zero distributional pressure for $u$, and for every $\varphi\in C^1([0,T];V)$ vanishing near $T$,
$$-\int_0^T(u,\varphi')_{L^2}\,dt+\int_0^T\bigl(a_\nu(u,\varphi)+c(u;u,\varphi)\bigr)\,dt-\int_0^Tb(\varphi',P)\,dt=\int_0^T(f,\varphi)_{L^2}\,dt+(u_0,\varphi(0))_{L^2}.$$
This pressure is a distribution; the assertion does not place $p$ in $L^{4/3}(0,T;Q)$.

For the discrete assertions, further assume that $D$ is polyhedral. Let $\mathcal T_j$ be matching shape-regular MINI meshes with $h_j\to0$, and let $0=t_0^j<\cdots<t_{N_j}^j=T$ have maximum step $\tau_{\max,j}\to0$. On each mesh take $u_{h,j}^0=P_{Z_j}u_0$ and any actual scheme solution $(u_{h,j}^n,p_{h,j}^n)$. Write $\overline u_{h,j}(t)=u_{h,j}^n$ and $\overline p_{h,j}(t)=p_{h,j}^n$ on $(t_{n-1}^j,t_n^j]$. For any subsequence for which $\overline u_{h,j}$ converges to $u$ as in [[thm-na-mini-navier-stokes-be-subsequential-limit]], define $P_{h,j}^0=0$, $P_{h,j}^m=\sum_{n=1}^m\tau_n^jp_{h,j}^n$, and let $P_{h,j}$ be the continuous piecewise-affine interpolant of these nodal values. If $\max_n\|u_{h,j}^n\|_{L^2}\le U_j$ and $\|\overline u_{h,j}\|_{L^2V}\le E_j$, then the uniform MINI inf-sup lower bound $\beta>0$ gives
$$\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\|P_{h,j}(t)\|_{L^2}\le\beta^{-1}\bigl(2C_PU_j+C_P\sqrt T F+2\nu\sqrt T E_j+C_cT^{1/4}U_j^{1/2}E_j^{3/2}\bigr).$$
Along a further subsequence, $P_{h,j}\rightharpoonup P$ in $L^2(0,T;Q)$. The piecewise-constant pressures converge to $p$ as $Q$-valued time distributions: for every $q\in Q$ and $\eta\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$,
$$\int_0^T(\overline p_{h,j}(t),q)_{L^2}\eta(t)\,dt\longrightarrow(\langle p,\eta\rangle,q)_{L^2}.$$
No relation between mesh size and maximum time step is imposed. These conclusions give pressure primitives and time-distribution convergence, not an instantaneous pressure regularity estimate.

Finally, let $u_t^{\mathrm{full}}$ denote the distributional derivative of $u$ as a $V^*$-valued distribution, using the embedding $L^2(D)^d\hookrightarrow V^*$. For this $u$, the pressure-bearing $L^{4/3}(0,T;Q)$ clause holds if and only if $u_t^{\mathrm{full}}$ is represented by an $L^{4/3}(0,T;V^*)$ Bochner function. This criterion concerns the actual full derivative, not an extension of its restriction to $V_\sigma$.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice.

Split the unit square by its diagonal into $K_1=\{0<y<x<1\}$ and $K_2=\{0<x<y<1\}$. For unit permeability and $f=1$ on $K_1$, $f=-1$ on $K_2$, the hybrid solution has
$$u_1=\tfrac12\theta_1,\quad u_2=-\tfrac12\theta_2,\quad p_1=\tfrac1{12},\quad p_2=-\tfrac1{12},\quad\lambda=0,$$
where $\theta_1(x,y)=(x-1,y)$ and $\theta_2(x,y)=(x,y-1)$. The local elimination equations reduce to $t_K/6-p_K+\lambda=0$, $t_1=1/2$, $t_2=-1/2$, and $t_1+t_2=0$; changing $\lambda$ shifts both pressures by the same constant and is precisely the gauge.

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice.

Split the unit square by its diagonal into $K_1=\{0<y<x<1\}$ and $K_2=\{0<x<y<1\}$. For unit permeability and $f=1$ on $K_1$, $f=-1$ on $K_2$, the hybrid solution has
$$u_1=\tfrac12\theta_1,\quad u_2=-\tfrac12\theta_2,\quad p_1=\tfrac1{12},\quad p_2=-\tfrac1{12},\quad\lambda=0,$$
where $\theta_1(x,y)=(x-1,y)$ and $\theta_2(x,y)=(x,y-1)$. The local elimination equations reduce to $t_K/6-p_K+\lambda=0$, $t_1=1/2$, $t_2=-1/2$, and $t_1+t_2=0$; changing $\lambda$ shifts both pressures by the same constant and is precisely the gauge.

1.1 Each cell has area $1/2$. The field $\theta_1=(x-1,y)$ has zero normal component on $x=1$ and $y=0$, and unit integrated outward flux on the diagonal from $K_1$; $\theta_2=(x,y-1)$ has zero normal component on $x=0$ and $y=1$, and unit integrated outward flux on the diagonal from $K_2$. Their divergences are both $2$, so $\int_{K_i}\operatorname{div}\theta_i=1$ by [F3]. The two zero-boundary conditions and the single free facet degree of freedom make each $\theta_i$ a basis of its local space by [F4]. Direct integration gives $\int_{K_1}|\theta_1|^2=\int_0^1\int_0^x((x-1)^2+y^2)\,dy\,dx=\tfrac16,$ and reflection symmetry gives $\int_{K_2}|\theta_2|^2=1/6$. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Write $u_i=t_i\theta_i$. The cell balances in [F1] give $t_1=\int_{K_1}f=1/2$ and $t_2=\int_{K_2}f=-1/2$. For a local test $v_i=s\theta_i$, its integrated divergence is $s$ and its interior outward flux is $s$. The first hybrid equation is therefore $t_i s/6-p_i s+\lambda s=0$ for every real $s$, equivalently $t_i/6-p_i+\lambda=0$. The jump equation is $t_1+t_2=0$, which the balance values satisfy. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Solving the local equations gives $p_1=1/12+\lambda$ and $p_2=-1/12+\lambda$. Since the cells have equal area, their global mean is $\lambda$; choose the mean-zero gauge $\lambda=0$ to obtain the stated pressures. After local elimination the single skeleton equation is $t_1+t_2=0$, independent of $\lambda$, so its one-dimensional nullspace consists exactly of common constant shifts. This is the constant gauge described in [F2]. [A1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

The two zero-boundary conditions and the single free facet degree of freedom make each $\theta_i$ a basis of its local space by [F4]. Direct integration gives $\int_{K_1}|\theta_1|^2=\int_0^1\int_0^x((x-1)^2+y^2)\,dy\,dx=\tfrac16,$ and reflection symmetry gives $\int_{K_2}|\theta_2|^2=1/6$. [given, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 Write $u_i=t_i\theta_i$. The cell balances in [F1] give $t_1=\int_{K_1}f=1/2$ and $t_2=\int_{K_2}f=-1/2$. For a local test $v_i=s\theta_i$, its integrated divergence is $s$ and its interior outward flux is $s$. The first hybrid equation is therefore $t_i s/6-p_i s+\lambda s=0$ for every real $s$, equivalently $t_i/6-p_i+\lambda=0$. The jump equation is $t_1+t_2=0$, which the balance values satisfy. [F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Solving the local equations gives $p_1=1/12+\lambda$ and $p_2=-1/12+\lambda$. Since the cells have equal area, their global mean is $\lambda$; choose the mean-zero gauge $\lambda=0$ to obtain the stated pressures. After local elimination the single skeleton equation is $t_1+t_2=0$, independent of $\lambda$, so its one-dimensional nullspace consists exactly of common constant shifts. This is the constant gauge described in [F2]. [A1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
